channel.title: The Brief — Adam's News
channel.description: Every story from Adam's three daily briefs (9 AM / 5 PM / 10 PM CT) as its own item, readable right in your feed reader, with a link to the original article.

item.title: Putin rules out any ceasefire after Kerch Bridge hit, as Berlin allies rally behind Kyiv
item.description:
Vladimir Putin said on Thursday he will not agree to a ceasefire or any deal to stop hitting energy infrastructure, after Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge — the only direct link between Russia and occupied Crimea — for the third time in four days. Hours later, allies gathered in Berlin to back Kyiv, announcing a prisoner swap for next week and pledging billions more in support.
The overnight strike hit the bridge's rail section with Ukrainian-made Neptune missiles, according to Ukraine's Defence Ministry, halting train traffic while Russian authorities assessed the damage. Rail service resumed on Thursday afternoon, the Moscow-appointed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said. The road section was already out of action after a large section of road deck and an arch collapsed in Tuesday's strike. Ukraine says Russia will now have to reroute fuel and ammunition supplies overland, where "our drones are waiting for the cargo," its Defence Ministry said. Russia's Defence Ministry said its air defences intercepted 53 Ukrainian drones over 10 Russian regions overnight, and Crimea's occupation authorities announced free Kerch–Kavkaz ferries from November 20 to replace the crossing.
Putin, speaking to reporters in Shenzhen after his trilateral meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, was blunt. "After the strike on the Crimean Bridge, we will not be agreeing" to a cease-fire or any agreement "to not hit the energy infrastructure," he said, according to the New York Post. "We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that," he told reporters, the Associated Press reports. He also claimed the bridge was "exclusively civilian" infrastructure and said he had ordered it closed to the transport of military hardware or ammunition — even as the AP notes the 19-kilometre bridge is a key route for military and civilian supplies to Crimea, which Russia uses to support frontline troops.
Russia answered overnight with anti-ship missiles and 98 drones at Ukraine, with hits recorded at 18 locations, according to Ukrainian authorities cited by the AP. At least 10 people were reported wounded and damage was recorded in 12 regions, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. The strikes came a day after daytime drone attacks on Kyiv, including one that crashed near the Dutch Embassy.
The two sides are arguing over the same logic from opposite ends. Kyiv says the bridge and refinery strikes are retaliation for Russia's nightly campaign against Ukrainian power plants and cities, and will continue until Russia stops hitting Ukrainian infrastructure. Moscow calls the bridge civilian and vows retaliation, while its own energy strikes continue. Washington is split from its European allies on the strategy: at Tuesday's Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting in Brussels, Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby argued the deep strikes have not shortened the war and hardened Russian resolve — a position Germany and Britain rejected the same day, and which Berlin's summit effectively overruled by doubling down on support.
In Berlin, the Coalition of the Willing — more than 40 countries — met with President Zelenskyy and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said "a Yalta-style format will not bring about peace" and that any negotiations must include both Ukraine and Europe, a direct answer to the Shenzhen summit's silence on Ukraine. NATO allies reaffirmed €70 billion in military assistance for 2026, with comparable support planned for 2027, and the European Commission's Ursula von der Leyen cited a new €45 billion loan and a 22nd sanctions package on the way. Kushner announced a new prisoner exchange in the week of November 23, covering more than 1,000 prisoners of war, after talks resumed in Abu Dhabi under US mediation. He also said Washington had brought Russia around to the concept of Article 5-style security guarantees for Ukraine — though no Russian official has been quoted accepting that, and a proposed four-party format bringing together Ukraine, Europe, the US and Russia has no agreed date, agenda or location. Trump joined the Berlin meeting by phone and, according to Politico, asked why allies keep spending millions on military support for Kyiv.
For people on the ground, the winter war is now a daily cycle with no safe hours. In Kyiv, homes are getting only around four hours of electricity a day and daytime drone attacks have removed the idea of a safe part of the day. In Crimea, losing the bridge's rail link — even temporarily — squeezes supplies to a peninsula already under a state of emergency over power outages and fuel shortages, with ferries now the fallback.
In short: Ukraine's third bridge strike in four days killed any talk of an energy ceasefire — Putin said so himself in Shenzhen — while Berlin answered with more money, more drones and a prisoner swap next week. The diplomacy is moving, but the two sides are further apart on a ceasefire than they were a week ago. Watch whether Russia's promised retaliation materialises, and whether the prisoner swap goes ahead as announced.
*Sources: Associated Press via WPTF, New York Post, Pollar, tut0ugh.news, The Library Estate*
Source: wptf.com.

item.title: Houthi missile hits Riyadh's tallest tower as Saudi Arabia braces for a six-month Yemen war
item.description:
A suspected Houthi missile struck the PIF Tower in Riyadh early on Thursday — the kingdom's tallest skyscraper and headquarters of its sovereign wealth fund — blowing out windows across seven to eight floors and bending parts of its metal facade. It was the second time in less than two weeks that a Houthi attack damaged a landmark in the capital's financial district, and it came as Reuters reported Saudi war planners now expect the Yemen campaign to last up to six months, well into 2026.
Residents of the Saudi capital were woken by a loud boom in the early hours of Thursday. Entrances to the King Abdullah Financial District were closed and people were evacuated, with ambulances and fire trucks at the scene; no injuries were reported. Saudi Arabia's civil defence said a Houthi attack on a tower in the financial centre caused material damage to several floors and nearby buildings, and state news agency SPA published a photograph showing the PIF Tower, though officials did not name the building. Three sources familiar with the matter told Reuters the 80-storey tower — the tallest in the financial district, housing the Public Investment Fund, which manages more than $900 billion in assets — had been hit by an incoming Houthi missile. The Saudi-led coalition said it had "dealt with a missile threat" launched towards Riyadh, adding that its initial assessment showed debris had fallen and material damage had been reported. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted Riyadh's international airport and the financial district with cruise missiles, as well as Khamis Mushait and Abha in the south, though the Houthis did not immediately confirm the PIF Tower specifically.
The strike is the second hit on a financial-district landmark in eleven days, after a November 8 attack damaged state oil giant Aramco's building. The Houthis have been targeting Saudi airports and oil infrastructure since Yemen's frozen civil war reignited in July, and on the ground in Yemen they have seized swathes of territory from the Saudi-backed government, forcing a major retreat from the Bab el-Mandeb coast at the weekend to defend Aden.
The two sides read the war very differently. Riyadh, according to two Western officials briefed by the Saudis and cited by Reuters, now expects the campaign against the Houthis to last up to six months into 2027, with the goal of achieving territorial gains for Yemen's internationally recognised government before entering any negotiations — a calculation that subordinates diplomacy entirely to battlefield outcomes. A third source familiar with the Saudi plans confirmed the accounts. The same reporting says US offensive support — intelligence sharing, precision-guided munitions and targeting assistance that the Trump administration has so far withheld — could compress the ground campaign from months to weeks, but no such authorisation has been granted. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper in Riyadh on Wednesday, Cooper's third publicly reported visit since the Yemen conflict resumed. The Houthis, meanwhile, say they will continue under a principle of "siege for siege, airport for airport, and escalation for escalation," and have warned airlines and shipping companies to avoid Saudi airports and waters.
For ordinary people, the war is now hitting the symbols of Saudi Arabia's economic ambitions. The King Abdullah Financial District — home to the stock exchange and global firms such as Goldman Sachs — was closed to visitors after the attack, and the strike is a fresh blow to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's plans to develop and diversify the economy, Reuters notes. In Yemen, the fighting grinds on around Taiz, where authorities accuse the Houthis of blocking medicine shipments, and displacement continues. In the Gulf, no new attacks were reported on Thursday beyond Wednesday's incidents, and oil steadied — Brent around $92 a barrel and WTI around $82–83 — as tanker tracking showed flows out of the Persian Gulf still below pre-war levels, with more than half of Gulf tankers now moving oil via ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, according to Vortexa.
In short: the Houthis can now hit the heart of Riyadh's financial district, and Saudi Arabia is settling in for a long war rather than a quick campaign — up to six months, by its own planners' reckoning, unless Washington agrees to help on offence. Watch whether the US authorises the offensive support Riyadh wants, and whether Houthi forces keep closing on Aden.
*Sources: TBS News (Reuters), SRN News (Reuters), The Library Estate, House of Saud (Reuters), OilPrice.com*
Source: tbsnews.net.

item.title: Anthropic's shares (Nasdaq: ANT) closed at $97.17 on Thursday, up about 17% on the $83 IPO price, after opening at $111.50 — a 34% premium — and peaking at $115.10 just before noon
item.description:
The stock slipped as low as $92.72 during the day and was trading around $95.60 by mid-afternoon. More than 846 million shares changed hands, ahead of the 522 million traded on SpaceX's opening day in June, making ANT the most actively traded name on the Nasdaq. At the $111.50 open, Reuters put Anthropic's market value at about $2 trillion. The offering raised about $81.3 billion, the largest IPO on record, and underwriters have the option to buy up to 147 million more shares, which would take the total to $93.5 billion.
*Sources: Invezz, Motley Fool*
Source: invezz.com.

item.title: Nvidia fell 3.30% on Thursday to close at $145.98, after opening at $152.92 and touching $158.13 intraday — a sixth straight down session, roughly 40% below its October record of $243.37
item.description:
Volume hit 311.8 million shares, about 95% above its three-month average. The slide continued despite the record $115.8 billion quarter reported Tuesday. New today: UBS cut its price target to $220 from $240 — its second cut in three days — and securities firm Hagens Berman updated its Nvidia class-action investigation, with an expanded class period of December 19, 2024 to November 12, 2026 and a January 8, 2027 lead-plaintiff deadline. Moody's also cut its outlook on Nvidia to stable from positive.
*Sources: Motley Fool, Finnhub, WCIA / Hagens Berman*
Source: fool.com.

item.title: Google's Gemini can now work through Mac tasks in the background
item.description:
Google added computer-use to Gemini for Mac: the app can now use apps, files and websites to complete multi-step tasks in a background window while you work in the foreground, with a live preview and the ability to pause it and approve key actions. It runs on Apple-silicon Macs on macOS Sequoia 15.0 or later, in English in the US, for Google AI Plus, Pro and Ultra subscribers (plans from $4.99/month). Apple is also due to warn users more clearly about the risks of giving apps unrestricted access to their data when macOS 27.3 lands.
*Source: MacRumors*
Source: macrumors.com.

item.title: GreyNoise has now logged 192 Java4Shell-shaped requests from six IP addresses since November 17, with no successful intrusions on its sensors
item.description:
WatchTowr's honeypots have received blind exploit attempts, Cloudflare saw one scanner return about 17 hours after an initial probe with the exploit trigger while posing as Chrome, and Previdian logged nine attempts from six IPs on November 18–19. Vendors are still catching up: Red Hat shipped its RHEL 8/9/10 OpenJDK errata on Thursday, Keycloak shipped fixed container images, and Cloudflare added WAF rules. Cisco lists more than a dozen affected products with no fixed releases yet, and Siemens lists Industrial Edge Management products as affected with no fixes available. The flaw is still not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Note: one SecurityWeek headline reads "Exploited in the Wild," but its own reporting describes probing and attempts only — no confirmed compromise.
*Sources: SecurityWeek, CyberSixt, Abijita*
Source: securityweek.com.

item.title: Netanyahu trial: High Court struck out the petition — prosecutors can cross-examine Mandelblit
item.description:
Israel's High Court on Thursday struck out the prosecution's petition over restrictions on questioning defence witnesses, finding the defence's change of position had already secured the practical result prosecutors sought. Prosecutors are free to cross-examine former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit and future defence witnesses under the arrangement adopted by the Jerusalem District Court on Wednesday, and Sunday's hearing is cancelled. But the court — Supreme Court President Isaac Amit and Justices Yael Willner and Khaled Kabub — did not settle the broader legal question, calling it "a substantial question" while concluding this petition was no longer the right setting to resolve it. Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara is due before the trial panel on November 25.
*Source: JBizNews*
Source: jbiznews.com.

item.title: Trump, Xi and Putin hold first-ever three-way summit — and leave with a declaration, not a deal
item.description:
The leaders of the United States, China and Russia sat down together for the first time ever on Thursday in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC summit. The meeting lasted about 90 minutes, started nearly two hours late, and ended with a four-point joint statement the three leaders called a "peace declaration" — but no agreement on Ukraine, Iran, or nuclear weapons.
The declaration, published by China's Xinhua news agency and the Kremlin, commits the three countries to four things: reforming the United Nations so it can "respond more effectively to global challenges"; increasing the production and supply of refined petroleum products; limiting the International Criminal Court's reach, saying the court and "other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction"; and holding a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation, reaffirming that "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought." Strikingly, the document does not mention Ukraine or Iran at all, sets no timelines, and creates no new treaty — the last US-Russia arms pact, New START, expired in February and remains lapsed.
The one concrete result of the day came before the three-way session, in Trump's bilateral meeting with Xi: the US and China agreed to extend their trade truce, according to the Globe and Mail, CNBC and Bloomberg. Neither side said how long the extension runs or on what terms, and China's own readout mentioned no extension details. The truce agreed in Busan in October 2025 had been due to run until January 10, 2027, after tariffs between the two countries peaked at 145 percent on the American side and 125 percent on the Chinese side. Trump left Shenzhen for Washington soon after the talks ended, without speaking to reporters.
The two sides of the room read the day very differently. Supporters of the format called it historic in itself: Henry Huiyao Wang, a former senior adviser to China's government, told USA Today that "the summit is more than symbolic" and that "face-to-face dialogue of this kind can help calm down a lot of the world's conflicts." Skeptics said the substance was thin and the direction troubling: Jonathan Eyal of the Royal United Services Institute said "just about the only substantial outcome of the Shenzhen summit was the rejection of international law and institutions such as the International Court of Justice," and called it "a summit supposedly designed to deal with global questions, but one which ended up with an outright rejection of globalization." Ukraine's President Zelenskyy had warned in October that he did not want the meeting to turn into "'Yalta 2, 3, 4,' with a redistribution of influence" — a reference to the 1945 conference that carved up post-war Europe — and Putin, for his part, said there was nothing "wrong with Yalta." Xi described nuclear weapons as "the sword of Damocles hanging over humanity," according to Chinese state media.
For ordinary people, the immediate effects are limited but real. The pledge to boost refined-oil supplies, if it amounts to anything, could eventually ease fuel prices — but there is no mechanism or deadline attached, so nothing changes at the pump today. The trade-truce extension matters more directly: without it, US-China tariffs could have snapped back toward the triple-digit levels of last year, which would have raised prices on electronics, clothing and countless other goods. And for Ukrainians, the summit's silence on their war is the story: the three most powerful leaders in the world met, talked about Ukraine behind closed doors, and said nothing about it in public.
In short: a historic photo-op with a real document attached, but the document is promises, not deals — no Ukraine plan, no Iran plan, no nuclear treaty, and a trade-truce extension with no published terms. The test now is whether the promised nuclear-risk dialogue ever gets a date.
*Sources: USA Today, The Times, WorldPulseWire*
Source: usatoday.com.
item.content:encoded:
The leaders of the United States, China and Russia sat down together for the first time ever on Thursday in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC summit. The meeting lasted about 90 minutes, started nearly two hours late, and ended with a four-point joint statement the three leaders called a "peace declaration" — but no agreement on Ukraine, Iran, or nuclear weapons.

The declaration, published by China's Xinhua news agency and the Kremlin, commits the three countries to four things: reforming the United Nations so it can "respond more effectively to global challenges"; increasing the production and supply of refined petroleum products; limiting the International Criminal Court's reach, saying the court and "other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction"; and holding a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation, reaffirming that "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought." Strikingly, the document does not mention Ukraine or Iran at all, sets no timelines, and creates no new treaty — the last US-Russia arms pact, New START, expired in February and remains lapsed.

The one concrete result of the day came before the three-way session, in Trump's bilateral meeting with Xi: the US and China agreed to extend their trade truce, according to the Globe and Mail, CNBC and Bloomberg. Neither side said how long the extension runs or on what terms, and China's own readout mentioned no extension details. The truce agreed in Busan in October 2025 had been due to run until January 10, 2027, after tariffs between the two countries peaked at 145 percent on the American side and 125 percent on the Chinese side. Trump left Shenzhen for Washington soon after the talks ended, without speaking to reporters.

The two sides of the room read the day very differently. Supporters of the format called it historic in itself: Henry Huiyao Wang, a former senior adviser to China's government, told USA Today that "the summit is more than symbolic" and that "face-to-face dialogue of this kind can help calm down a lot of the world's conflicts." item.title: Kerch Bridge hit for the third time this week as Russia pounds Kyiv in daylight
item.description:
Ukraine struck Russia's Kerch Bridge — the only direct link between Russia and occupied Crimea — for the third time this week early on Thursday, halting rail traffic just as Vladimir Putin was about to sit down with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. Hours later, Russian drones were hitting Kyiv in broad daylight, including a drone that crashed near the Dutch Embassy and one that struck a three-storey building.
The bridge attack came days after a section of the road bridge collapsed following strikes on Monday and Tuesday. CNN reports that rail traffic was halted on Thursday morning and resumed in the afternoon, according to Russia's transport ministry, which said there were no casualties. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin told state media that individual sections of the bridge could reopen "within one or two months," and the Kremlin said it would be rebuilt "better than before." President Zelenskyy has described the bridge strikes — carried out, he says, exclusively with Ukraine-made weapons — as the seventh stage of an "unprecedented operation in response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure." Speaking to reporters in Shenzhen after the trilateral meeting, Putin threatened Ukraine with retaliation and claimed, despite ample evidence to the contrary, that the bridge serves "purely peaceful purposes."
Meanwhile Kyiv came under a renewed drone assault on Thursday afternoon, the eighth air-raid alert since overnight. The Kyiv Independent reports a Russian drone crashed near the Dutch Embassy, damaging cars and a security post and shattering windows, and a drone struck a three-storey building in daylight as Russia extends its barrages from overnight into daytime hours, often using newer jet-powered Shahed-type drones that leave residents little warning. In the Kyiv region, a woman was killed when a house in the Bucha district was partially destroyed, and four people were injured in the Vyshhorod district, including a child; 29 homes were damaged there. Overnight, Russia also hit two power substations in Odesa, a fuel storage facility in Chornomorsk, a cargo ship at the port of Odesa, and a substation in Sumy, according to Russia's defence ministry.
The two sides are fighting over the same logic from opposite ends. Kyiv says it is hitting the bridge and Russian refineries because Russia keeps hitting Ukrainian power plants and cities — the bridge is a military supply artery to Crimea, and Ukraine says it will keep striking Russian infrastructure until Russia stops striking Ukrainian infrastructure. Moscow calls the bridge civilian and threatens retaliation, while its own nightly campaign against Ukraine's energy grid continues; the UK government, meanwhile, announced on Wednesday it will gift Ukraine more than 1,000 long-range strike drones, some able to fly over 1,000 km carrying heavy warheads. The Coalition of the Willing — Ukraine's key allies — also met in Berlin on Thursday, with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner attending.
For people on the ground, the bridge strikes and the Kyiv attacks are two halves of the same winter war. In Crimea, Russian-installed authorities already imposed a state of emergency over the summer because of power outages and fuel shortages, and losing the bridge's rail link — even temporarily — squeezes the peninsula's supplies further. In Kyiv, the power crisis keeps deepening: many homes are getting only around four hours of electricity a day, and the daytime drone attacks mean there is no longer a safe part of the day.
In short: Ukraine took out a chunk of Russia's most symbolic supply line for the third time in a week, Russia answered by hitting Kyiv in daylight, and both sides are now trading infrastructure strikes with winter closing in. Watch whether the bridge's rail link holds and whether the Coalition of the Willing meeting produces new air-defence pledges.
*Sources: CNN, Kyiv Independent, shelter.in.ua*
Source: cnn.com.

item.title: Iran hits Kuwait and Bahrain again, another tanker struck — and a US carrier leaves the Gulf
item.description:
Iran widened its attacks across the Gulf on Wednesday, firing drones at a US airbase in Kuwait and launching fresh strikes on Bahrain, a day after American jets hit an Iranian missile site on Qeshm Island. At the same time, another tanker was hit in the Strait of Hormuz, and the US Navy pulled one of its three aircraft carriers out of the region.
Iran's army said its drones targeted Patriot missile systems and launch platforms at Ali Al-Salem Air Base in Kuwait, according to state broadcaster IRIB, and both Kuwait and Bahrain said they intercepted the attacks. Neither country reported damage or casualties. It was Iran's first attack on Kuwait since September, and Bahrain has now faced four Iranian attacks in six days. The strikes came a day after the US hit an IRGC missile launch site on Qeshm Island, which a US official described as a "self-defence" strike. Iran says its attacks are retaliation for that strike; the US has not announced further strikes.
On the water, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said an unknown projectile struck a tanker's engine room about six nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, at 16:45 UTC on Wednesday, and that all crew were safe and accounted for as of early Thursday. That follows Tuesday evening's hit on the Navig8 Messi, an ADNOC Logistics tanker struck 13 nautical miles off Oman, leaving one crew member missing and 11 injured, and the Panama-flagged LPG tanker Tara Gas, struck twice in two days with one Indian seafarer missing. Iran's army claims three tankers hit naval mines and caught fire — a claim Reuters and other outlets could not confirm — while UKMTO describes the strikes as unknown projectiles. The mechanism is unresolved, but the pattern is not: about 18 confirmed attacks on commercial vessels in and around the strait this month alone.
The two sides' accounts diverge sharply. Tehran says it is responding to American aggression and warns ships to coordinate passage with Iranian authorities, effectively claiming control of the strait; Washington says it is escorting ships through in defiance of that claim and calls the Qeshm strike self-defence. Gulf states are caught in the middle: Kuwait's foreign ministry called the attacks a "flagrant violation of sovereignty," the GCC chief held Iran responsible, and the Arab League asked the UN Security Council to act. Meanwhile a Navy official told CBS News the USS George Washington has left the Middle East for the 7th Fleet, leaving the USS George H.W. Bush and USS Theodore Roosevelt in the region.
The human and economic impact is spreading. The International Energy Agency's World Energy Outlook called the Hormuz crisis the "largest threat" to energy security in history — the strait carried about a quarter of global oil flows before the war. Oil prices actually fell on Wednesday — Brent to $91.95 and WTI to $83.26, its lowest since August 26 — after a big US crude stockpile build, but they remain hostage to the next incident. Gulf countries are facing mounting pressure on oil exports, and flight cancellations in Saudi Arabia continue as the Houthis keep firing: the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a Houthi cruise missile headed for southern Saudi Arabia, while Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claimed cruise missiles hit King Khalid International Airport and a Riyadh financial centre.
In short: the tit-for-tat is now a daily cycle — US strike, Iranian retaliation on Gulf allies, another tanker hit — and with one American carrier gone, the question is whether the remaining two are enough to keep the strait open, or whether Iran's mine and drone campaign will keep choking the world's most important oil chokepoint.
*Sources: NY Post, Dubai Standard, Mappr*
Source: nypost.com.

item.title: Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, above its $70–78 range, and starts trading today on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT
item.description:
The offering was upsized to 980 million shares, raising about $81.3 billion — the largest IPO in history, eclipsing SpaceX. The company is valued at roughly $1.5 trillion fully diluted, with Amazon set to hold about 14.7% and Google 13.7% after the offering. The filing shows a revenue run rate of about $81 billion as of October 31, but also roughly $900 billion in multi-year compute and infrastructure commitments. First trade comes after the 9:30 a.m. ET open, once Nasdaq's opening auction clears.
*Source: TradingView / dpa-AFX*
Source: tradingview.com.

item.title: Nvidia shares were up about 3.7% in early trading Thursday, to around $156.50, after closing Wednesday at $150.96 — down 2.89% and about 38% below the October record
item.description:
The rebound comes as scrutiny intensifies: the SEC is examining whether Nvidia misled investors in its disclosures, according to a Reuters report citing the Wall Street Journal, and House Energy and Commerce Committee chair Brett Guthrie has demanded interim CEO Colette Kress brief the panel by December 2 on export controls and safeguards. Separately, Semafor reports a faction of Nvidia's board is still pushing to bring back ousted CEO Jensen Huang, despite chairman Harvey Jones saying reinstatement is not under consideration — and Nvidia said on its earnings call it will not immediately file its 10-Q quarterly report, breaking with usual practice. Huang is due before three House committees on December 1.
*Sources: Finnhub, ad-hoc-news*
Source: finnhub.io.

item.title: Grand Theft Auto VI launched today, November 19, on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, with a 99 Metascore — tying The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as the highest-rated game in Metacritic history
item.description:
The PS5 version sits at 99 from 150 critic reviews, 100% positive; OpenCritic shows a 99 top-critic average with 99% recommending. The game costs $79.99 standard / $99.99 Ultimate Edition, and Sensor Tower estimates over 17 million copies sold already for more than $1.65 billion. Take-Two shares rose 6.5% on Wednesday. The launch hasn't been flawless: players are reporting glitches, crashes and a softlock in an early mission, and there's still no PC version announced. The game also leads The Game Awards 2026 nominations with eight, including Game of the Year.
*Sources: NME, BusinessWorld*
Source: nme.com.

item.title: Attackers have started probing for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), the OpenJDK Base64 memory-corruption flaw, but no successful intrusion has been reported
item.description:
GreyNoise counted 187 trigger-shaped requests from five IP addresses since November 17, aimed at paths like /login.action and /actuator/env, with no successful intrusions as of Thursday morning. Cloudflare said one IP probed a target with a "java4shell" user agent, then sent the exploit trigger about 17 hours later. Cisco, Elastic, Red Hat and Siemens have listed affected products; Oracle's fixed builds shipped November 17. The flaw is still not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Separately, Rapid7 has published proof-of-concept code for NGINX2Root (CVE-2026-123007), the decade-old HTTP/2 flaw fixed in NGINX 1.31.9 — and Synology says patches for affected DiskStation Manager versions are due November 20.
*Sources: CyberSixt, CyberSixt briefing*
Source: cybersixt.com.

item.title: Saudi Arabia replaced its Yemen coalition commander as Houthis advance on Aden (catch-up)
item.description:
King Salman replaced the commander of the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen on Monday, appointing Chief of Staff General Fayyad al-Ruwaili and reassigning Lieutenant General Fahd bin Hamad al-Salman as an adviser to the defence minister. The change came as Yemeni government forces withdrew from areas near the Bab el-Mandeb strait to concentrate on defending Aden, with Houthi forces reported about 100 km west of the city at Khor Omairh and around 25 km from government lines at Qawah. Fighting continued on Wednesday around Tur al-Bahah in Lahij and in Taiz, where authorities accuse the Houthis of blocking medicine shipments. No fighting inside Aden itself has been reported.
*Sources: Al Jazeera, The Library Estate*
Source: aljazeeranews-3fuh52rgrl.edgeone.app.

item.title: NOT NEW — Apple–Google Gemini deal:
item.description:
the "Apple taps Google Gemini to power Apple Intelligence" story is still circulating today, but it is the January 12, 2026 joint statement, not a new announcement.
No new reporting from Reuters, AP or Bloomberg confirms anything new. Do not treat it as fresh news.

item.title: Anthropic just priced the biggest IPO in history — $83 a share, about $81 billion raised
item.description:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models, priced its initial public offering at $83 a share on Wednesday evening, raising about $81.31 billion and eclipsing SpaceX's June offering to become the largest stock-market debut on record. The shares start trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT.
Reuters reports the offering was upsized by about 19% to 980 million shares, up from the planned 825 million at $70–$78 a share, after a roadshow that drew demand several times the shares on offer. On a fully diluted basis the IPO values Anthropic at about $1.5 trillion, Reuters reports; on a non-diluted basis the valuation is about $1.1 trillion. The company is also raising $26 billion through a private placement at the IPO price, with strategic investors including Google, Microsoft, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron and TSMC. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters. Le Monde, citing the Wall Street Journal, puts the share count slightly lower at 956 million shares and $79.3 billion raised — the price, the valuation and the record are not in dispute.
The numbers behind the valuation are striking and, in the other direction, sobering. Anthropic's annualised revenue run rate reached $81 billion as of October 31, up $10 billion in a single month, Reuters reports, driven by Claude Code, its coding agent. It had 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 a year, up from more than 1,500 at the end of last year. Revenue rose 47% in the third quarter to $16.96 billion from the second quarter — but the company reported an operating loss of $567 million, after operating income of $974 million the previous quarter, and it spent nearly $9 billion on computing in the first half of 2026, nearly four times a year earlier, plus another $5 billion in the third quarter. It has committed to nearly $900 billion in computing spending with infrastructure partners including Amazon and Google, and its prospectus warns that some of those partners depend on third-party financing to buy chips and build data centres: "If such financing or support becomes unavailable or more costly, contracted capacity may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered."
What each side says: bulls argue the frontier is where the value accrues — Baillie Gifford's Peter Singlehurst, whose firm invested roughly $1.5 billion before the IPO, told Reuters Anthropic has "the highest probability of remaining at the frontier." Bears point to the spending: investors have grown increasingly concerned about debt-fuelled AI infrastructure expansion, and Anthropic's own filing warns its models could develop capabilities faster than it can evaluate them. The competitive picture is mixed — OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra accounted for about 13% of enterprise AI spending tracked by Ramp, against about 8% for Anthropic's Claude Fable, according to data cited by Reuters in September, though Anthropic's revenue run rate was ahead at the time. OpenAI is expected to pursue its own listing as early as next year. And Anthropic's own chief executive, Dario Amodei, has publicly called for the industry to slow the pace of releasing increasingly powerful models.
For ordinary people, the direct impact is mostly indirect: this is the first major frontier AI lab to go public, and how ANT trades on Thursday will be read as a verdict on whether the AI buildout — the data centres, the chips, the power — is a durable boom or an overextended bet. That matters because the same buildout is behind the chip sell-off, the power-grid strain and the jobs questions in the AI economy. Individual investors were supposed to get up to 20% of the shares offered.
In short: Anthropic priced above its range at $83, raised roughly $81 billion — the largest IPO ever — and debuts Thursday at a ~$1.5 trillion valuation, even as its own filings flag $900 billion in compute commitments and a return to operating losses. Watch how ANT trades on its first day, and whether it steadies or deepens the AI-stock sell-off.
Sources:
Source: kz1023.com.

item.title: Iran claims three more tankers hit mines on Wednesday evening — unverified, as the confirmed toll keeps rising
item.description:
Iran's military claimed on Wednesday evening that three more oil tankers caught fire after striking naval mines east of the Strait of Hormuz, hours after a confirmed attack on a UAE-operated tanker left one crew member missing and 11 injured. No vessel was named, no flag or owner identified, and Reuters could not independently confirm the evening claim — but the pattern of the day points to a Gulf shipping war that is getting harder, not easier, to contain.
The confirmed incident is the attack on the Liberian-flagged tanker Navig8 Messi, operated by ADNOC Logistics & Services, the shipping arm of Abu Dhabi's state oil company. The vessel was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles off Oman on Tuesday evening, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre, and video shared on social media shows the ship listing as flames and black smoke pour into the sky. ADNOC confirmed on Wednesday that one crew member is missing, 11 were injured and receiving medical care, and the rest were evacuated. The New York Post reports it is the second time the Navig8 Messi has been attacked in four months, and that there have been some 18 confirmed attacks on commercial vessels in and around the strait this month alone. A second vessel, the Panamanian-flagged LPG tanker Tara Gas, was struck twice off Oman's Musandam Peninsula this week and abandoned; one Indian seafarer from that ship is also still missing, so two crew members from two ships are now unaccounted for.
Iran's account of what is happening differs sharply from the shipping record. The Revolutionary Guard and Iran's army have said tankers caught fire after hitting mines while sailing unauthorised routes with their tracking systems off, and on Wednesday evening Iran's army said three "violating" tankers had struck mines and that passage through the waterway "must be coordinated with Iranian authorities," according to reports carried by ANI and Al Jazeera. Independent monitors, however, have noted a pattern of projectile strikes, and the UKMTO reports describe projectiles, not mines. The gap between what Iran claims and what anyone can verify is itself the story: Reuters could not confirm the evening claim, and no shipowner, flag state or insurer has stepped forward to say one of its hulls was hit.
What each side says: Iran says its attacks — including the drone strikes on US facilities in Bahrain and Kuwait this week — are retaliation for US drone surveillance and the US strike on a Revolutionary Guard missile site on Qeshm Island on Tuesday, and for an attack on Iranian communications towers. Washington has confirmed the Qeshm strike as self-defence and says further strikes are "quite unlikely," while sending a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the region. Analysts quoted by the Associated Press describe a deliberate, calibrated escalation: Hamidreza Azizi of the International Crisis Group wrote that "even if neither side intends to enter a broader confrontation, the accumulation of military incidents across multiple fronts increases the risk of miscalculation," while Danny Citrinowicz of Israel's Institute for National Security Studies said Iran's objective "is not necessarily to trigger an all-out war, but to steadily increase the military, economic, and political costs of maintaining the blockade." His conclusion: "As long as the U.S. naval blockade remains in place and no agreement is reached, further escalation will become increasingly difficult to avoid."
For ordinary people, the human cost is already concrete — two seafarers missing, 11 injured, crews abandoning burning ships — and the economic cost is creeping into fuel prices even as headline oil prices fall. Brent crude traded below $92 on Wednesday, down on a big US inventory build and the IEA's finding that global supply has surpassed demand, but shippers are paying more to move oil through the strait, and Iraq has resumed pumping oil to Turkey by pipeline specifically to avoid Hormuz. Mediation continues — Qatar says it met the Iranian side on Tuesday — but the fighting has now run for nine months with no agreement in sight.
In short: Iran claims three more tankers hit mines on Wednesday evening, but no one has independently confirmed it; what is confirmed is the ADNOC tanker strike that left one crew member missing and 11 hurt, plus a second missing seafarer from the Tara Gas. Analysts warn the pattern is deliberate escalation that risks a miscalculation. Watch whether any independent source confirms the evening mine claims, and whether Thursday's Shenzhen trilateral produces any movement on Iran.
Sources:
Source: nypost.com.

item.title: The Houthis are now positioned to threaten Aden from two sides, analysts say
item.description:
Houthi forces are likely attempting to capture Yemeni government positions on advantageous terrain near Jabal Kharaz, in a move that would set conditions to besiege and capture Aden, according to a new assessment from the Institute for the Study of War published on Wednesday. It is the sharpest warning yet that the southern port city — the seat of Yemen's internationally recognised government — is now the Houthis' objective, not just a distant threat.
Geolocated footage showed Houthi forces captured a Yemeni government defensive position east of Khour Umairah and south of Jabal Kharaz, along the Mokha–Aden road in Lahij governorate, on November 16, ISW reports. Houthi fighters separately engaged government-aligned forces in al-Maqatirah and Tur al-Bahah districts on November 17 and 18, suggesting they are simultaneously pressing Aden's northern and western flanks. By November 16 the Houthis had reached Khor Omairh, roughly 100 kilometres west of Aden, and fighting has resumed in Tur al-Bahah, described as Aden's first defensive line and about 80 kilometres from the city. No fighting inside Aden itself has been reported.
The advance follows a repositioning announced on November 15, when government and Southern forces withdrew from Dhubab airport and the Bab al-Mandeb area to defend Aden — a move they described as planned, but one that handed the Houthis the vacated coastal positions and consolidated their grip on the strategic strait. The Saudi-led coalition answered on Tuesday with a "precision operation" against 60 Houthi military targets in Sanaa, Hodeidah, Amran and Saada, including mountain tunnels used as workshops and storage for ballistic missiles and drone assembly facilities, according to coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki. The target count and claimed destruction have not been independently verified. Houthi health officials said at least 17 people were killed, including 15 in a strike on a sponge factory in Hodeidah, and spokesman Yahya Saree claimed 81 coalition strikes in 24 hours — none of it independently confirmed. The Houthis also kept up their own campaign against Saudi Arabia: ISW reports the group likely launched missiles and drones at Saudi critical infrastructure on November 17 and 18, and the coalition said it intercepted three Houthi cruise missiles and drones near Riyadh and one drone over southern Saudi Arabia.
What each side says: the coalition says its strikes are degrading Houthi missile and drone capabilities and neutralising the maritime threat. The Houthis say they are acting to compel Saudi Arabia to end military operations in Yemen and submit to their economic demands — ending Saudi support for the recognised government, lifting Saudi controls on Houthi-held ports and airports, and granting the Houthis control over Yemen's oil and gas resources, according to ISW. Meanwhile, further north, Taiz remains under siege: Al Jazeera's correspondent reported fierce fighting, villages on Jabal Sabr under complete siege, and Taiz authorities accusing the Houthis of blocking medicine shipments from Aden and confiscating supplies, with an appeal for UN intervention. The UN says more than 340,000 people have been displaced across Yemen since August.
For ordinary people, the stakes are immediate and grim. Aden is home to the government, the central bank and the main functioning port for the south; a siege would cut off food, fuel and medicine for hundreds of thousands of people, on top of a displacement crisis that has already uprooted more than 340,000 since August. In Taiz, civilians — mostly children and women, according to Al Jazeera's correspondent — are already under daily sniper fire. And the fighting is spilling into shipping: Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have announced a conditional return of three Gemini services to the Suez route from December or January, a first test of whether Red Sea transits can resume despite the Houthi advance on Bab al-Mandeb.
In short: the Houthis have taken ground on both flanks of Aden and, in ISW's assessment, are positioning to besiege the city — and the coalition's 60-target air campaign has not stopped the advance. Watch whether government forces hold Tur al-Bahah, whether the Houthis push closer to Aden, and whether the Suez test sailings actually happen.
Sources:
Source: thelibraryestate.com.

item.title: Nvidia posted a record quarter — and the stock fell anyway, for the fifth straight day
item.description:
Nvidia shares closed at $150.96 on Wednesday, down 2.9%, marking a fifth consecutive session of declines despite the company reporting quarterly results and revenue guidance that beat analysts' estimates. The stock opened at $159.19, up 2.4% from Tuesday's close, touched $159.70 in the morning, then slid all day to a low of $150.40 on heavy volume of about 340 million shares — roughly 117% above its three-month average, according to the Motley Fool.
The results themselves were, by any normal measure, a blowout: revenue of $115.8 billion in the third quarter of fiscal 2027, up 103% from a year earlier, with adjusted earnings of $2.68 a share against a $2.47 consensus, and fourth-quarter guidance of $130 billion. The company also announced a further $150 billion in share buybacks. But the market's verdict was the opposite of the numbers. The stock is now about 38% below its October 6 record close of $243.37, down roughly 30% over the past month, and the average analyst price target fell to $251.74 on Wednesday from $265.70 on Monday, according to Reuters-cited data. The S&P 500 closed down 0.2% and the Nasdaq rose 0.4% on the day, so Nvidia's fall was its own story, not the market's.
What each side says: the bull case is the fundamentals — record revenue, record guidance, the Vera Rubin platform described by the company as its fastest ramp ever, and a $150 billion buyback. The bear case, which is winning for now, is everything around the numbers: succession uncertainty after Jensen Huang's ousting (the board has said it does not intend to reinstate him, and Huang is due before congressional committees on December 1), tighter US chip-export rules for data centres in Southeast Asia, and broader valuation anxiety about AI infrastructure spending — the same anxiety hanging over Anthropic's IPO, priced the same evening. The Motley Fool notes investors are weighing the CEO transition and China-related regulatory scrutiny; the Associated Press reports the stock initially rose 2.7% after the results before erasing its gains and ending lower.
For ordinary people, the direct effect is mostly through retirement accounts and index funds — Nvidia is one of the largest weights in the S&P 500 — but the wider signal matters more: the market is no longer rewarding AI companies for growth alone. It wants to see who pays for the data centres, who runs the companies, and whether the spending ever turns into durable profit. Anthropic's debut on Thursday will be the next test of that question.
In short: Nvidia beat on revenue, earnings and guidance — and fell 2.9% anyway, its fifth straight down day and roughly 38% off its October peak. The market is pricing succession, China rules and AI-spending doubts, not the quarter. Watch whether Anthropic's trading debut steadies the AI trade or deepens the slide.
Sources:
Source: fool.com.

item.title: "Russian drone attack on Kyiv leaves three injured amid disputed reports of residential building strike" — h.ua
item.description:
Russian drones hit Kyiv again on Wednesday, injuring three people — one hospitalised — as debris fell in several districts, including on an unfinished building in Pecherskyi district and, according to the mayor, on the 11th floor of a 28-storey residential building, a claim the Kyiv City Military Administration disputed. Debris also set several trucks on fire at a commercial site, and morning strikes left debris in the Darnytskyi district. Ukraine hit back overnight: the General Staff confirmed Ukrainian drones struck the Ilysky and Afipsky oil refineries in Russia's Krasnodar region. Separately, Polish newspaper Rzeczpospolita reported on Wednesday that Russian intelligence services were preparing a sabotage and false-flag operation near Poland's border with Russia's Kaliningrad exclave in late October or early November, meant to blame Ukraine and undermine Western aid — single-source and unconfirmed. Coalition of the Willing leaders also met in Berlin on Wednesday to discuss Ukraine support and security guarantees.
Sources:
Source: en.h.ua.

item.title: "Conflicting agendas and a weakened Trump mark historic three-way summit" — Washington Post
item.description:
Thursday's first-ever trilateral between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin will bring three different agendas to one table, the Washington Post reports: Trump wants to focus on nuclear arms control, a potential legacy achievement, with the New START treaty expired since February and no formal limits on US and Russian arsenals; Putin sees an opening to discuss ending the war in Ukraine on his terms; Xi does not want to discuss either topic. Kremlin foreign-policy aide Yuri Ushakov said the countries are in intensive consultations over a draft joint statement, and it remains unclear whether one will be adopted. The schedule, per published reports: an APEC family photo at 9:30 a.m. local time, a Trump–Xi bilateral and working lunch at 12:45 p.m., and the closed-door trilateral at 2:30 p.m. local time, with Trump also expected to meet Putin one-on-one. Analysts still expect no substantive breakthroughs.
Sources:
Source: wallhop.io.

item.title: "Google Releases New Gemini 4 Neon: What to Know" — Chiang Rai Times
item.description:
Google announced Gemini 4 Neon on November 18, a new model in the Gemini 4 family aimed at demanding coding, analysis, science and agent work, positioned between the fast everyday model and the most capable one. It has a roughly one-million-token context window, four adjustable thinking levels, and paid API pricing starting at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. It is rolling out through the paid Gemini API, Google AI Studio and Google Antigravity for paid Pro and Ultra subscribers. Google says it is adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon and that its cost per task is 32% lower than Carbon's at the default setting — Google's claims, not independently verified.

item.title: "Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): OpenJDK RCE Vulnerability FAQ" — Tenable
item.description:
The Java4Shell picture moved a step closer to real-world attacks on Wednesday. Tenable's updated FAQ reports that GreyNoise has seen exploitation attempts against CVE-2026-114938 but has not confirmed any successful exploitation against its sensors, while VulnCheck says a full exploit is available to its customers and Immersive's Kevin Breen reports building one. Talos and CERT-EU report no in-the-wild exploitation yet, though Talos anticipates probing soon, and SANS Internet Storm Center discussed the flaw — alongside a new NGINX flaw, below — without raising its alert level. The flaw is still not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The fix remains the same: install your vendor's November Java update, or restart affected JVMs with the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics flag. Cloudflare has also published WAF protection for the flaw.
Sources:
Source: tenable.com.

item.title: "10-Year-Old NGINX HTTP/2 Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code on Servers" — The Hacker News
item.description:
A decade-old flaw in NGINX's HTTP/2 support, CVE-2026-123007, can let an attacker run code on servers with HTTP/2 enabled without logging in, The Hacker News reported on Wednesday. NGINX released version 1.31.9 today to fix it, and the flaw was found in part by an automated harness — Xint's tooling found four of the five NGINX flaws disclosed this week, including CVE-2026-123007. Talos anticipates probing soon, though no in-the-wild exploitation has been reported. If you run NGINX with HTTP/2, update.

item.title: "TfL Data Breach Exposes 265,000 Oyster Card Users' Personal Information" — ThreatCluster
item.description:
Transport for London reported a data breach affecting about 265,000 Oyster photocard users, according to a report published Wednesday. The breach was discovered on November 16, when customers received emails prompting them to create accounts despite already having them. Compromised data includes names, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth and security questions — but no passwords or financial information, the report says. TfL has taken the photocard website offline for investigation and reported the incident to the Information Commissioner's Office. Single-source report; TfL's own statement was not independently reviewed for this brief.

Source: threatcluster.io.

item.title: "Old Windows bug enables threat actor to steal data from over 1 million credit, debit cards" — Neowin
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers at Cybernews found an exposed server belonging to a threat actor attacking point-of-sale systems, Neowin reported on Wednesday. The campaign compromised more than 700 POS terminals across more than 20 countries and exposed at least one million credit and debit card records. The attacker exploited a privilege-escalation flaw in the Windows Common Log File System (CLFS) driver that Microsoft patched almost two years ago — but many POS terminals were never updated, because retailers worried about downtime and compatibility or simply did not prioritise patching. A reminder that the patch you skip is the one that gets used.
Source:
Source: neowin.net.

item.title: "France Is Blaming Iran for the Fridge Cyberattack" — Schneier on Security
item.description:
France is blaming Iran for the large-scale cyberattack on French supermarket refrigeration systems reported last month, according to Schneier on Security. The attack forced Danfoss controllers into defrost, reportedly spoiling food across around 150 Intermarché stores and dozens more, and French investigators had been hunting for who was behind it with no claim of responsibility. If the attribution holds, it would tie the incident directly to the Iran conflict rather than to a lone hacker or criminal group, as earlier reporting had suggested. Single-source; the French government's own statement was not independently reviewed for this brief.

item.title: "Russell Brand Faces Ban on Speaking to His Wife From Prison" — Parade
item.description:
The fallout from Russell Brand's prison statement kept growing on Wednesday. The British government asked Google to remove Brand's YouTube account after his wife Laura Gallacher read out a message from him on the couple's channel on Sunday, in which he said he was not guilty of the offences he was jailed for. Downing Street called the message "clearly appalling" and said it was being urgently investigated; prisoners are banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances. The Ministry of Justice has opened an investigation, and Brand could face restrictions on calls, visits and other privileges, as well as a review of his security classification. Gallacher visited him at HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire on Wednesday. Brand, 51, was convicted on November 5 of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and sentenced on November 9 to ten years and six months. No appeal has been announced.
Sources:
Source: parade.com.

item.title: Ukraine's drones have nearly halved Russia's oil refining — and the grid war is now raising nuclear fears
item.description:
Ukrainian drone attacks have slashed Russian oil refineries' combined crude processing by 45% since late October, according to industry estimates reported exclusively by Reuters on Wednesday — the clearest measure yet of how far Kyiv's long-range campaign has bitten. At the same time, Russia kept hitting Ukrainian cities, killing four people in Odesa, and nuclear safety regulators from 38 countries warned that the grid war is raising the risk of a nuclear accident this winter.
Reuters reports, citing two industry sources, that Russian refineries' crude processing has fallen to around 400,000 metric tons a day — about 3 million barrels a day — from more than 700,000 tons a day at the end of October. The attacks have now disrupted or halted operations at 15 of Russia's 35 major refineries, up from 9 in the middle of last week, including plants in Ryazan, Yaroslavl, Kirishi and the Volga region. The combined nominal capacity of the refineries affected since late October stands at around 500,000 tons a day, roughly 54% of Russia's total primary refining capacity. Russia is already facing domestic fuel shortages in some regions and restricted export capacity, Reuters reports, and reduced refining could tighten global fuel markets and hamper Moscow's ability to deliver on a deal to export diesel to the United States. The sources cautioned that because the reduction was gradual, average November processing is still above 500,000 tons a day — about 5% to 10% below September and October levels.
The refining squeeze follows nearly three weeks of near-daily Ukrainian drone strikes, capped by what Russia's Defence Ministry said on Monday was the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the full-scale invasion began — 1,441 drones claimed intercepted, a record. That barrage included the two-night operation that collapsed the road arch of the Kerch Bridge to Crimea, reported in yesterday's briefs. President Zelenskyy has claimed Ukraine has disabled more than 55% of Russian refining capacity; the industry sources cited by Reuters put the processing cut at 45%, a lower but independently sourced figure. Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" on October 11 that neither Moscow nor Kyiv acknowledged agreeing to; Ukrainian strikes eased for roughly two weeks, then intensified again as Russia ramped up its own drone and missile strikes.
Russia's answer on Wednesday was aimed at Ukrainian cities and the grid. Russian forces struck the centre of Odesa, the Black Sea port, in three waves, killing four people and injuring 13, according to regional officials cited by Reuters. Windows of residential buildings, cafes and shops were broken, a car was set on fire, and a residential building and an educational institution were damaged. President Zelenskyy said Shahed drones struck the centre of the city. The strikes came a day after Russia hit Kyiv's North and South bridges with seven ballistic missiles and as Ukraine's Energy Ministry counts more than 1,000 Russian strikes on energy facilities since September, leaving many Kyiv homes with power for only around four hours a day.
The grid campaign has now drawn a formal warning from nuclear regulators. Three international associations — HERCA, WENRA and NORA, representing regulators from 38 countries including all EU members, the United States, Britain, Canada and Japan — warned on Monday, in a joint statement reported by Reuters, that Russia's intensifying attacks on Ukraine's electricity infrastructure are increasing the risk of a nuclear accident this winter. Their concern is that reactors need reliable electricity to keep their fuel cool even when shut down, and prolonged outages force plants onto emergency generators. Per Strand, who heads HERCA and NORA, told Reuters that "the highest risk will be this winter for a nuclear accident," and described a nationwide blackout affecting all nine of Ukraine's operating reactors at once as the worst-case scenario. Ukraine's three working nuclear plants are expected to supply about 80% of the country's electricity this winter, according to Reuters — before the war, nuclear was just over half. The International Atomic Energy Agency said on Saturday that grid instability from military activity had forced several operating reactors to cut output in the preceding week, and that a drone had been detected about 350 metres from the South Ukraine plant. At Zaporizhzhia, Europe's largest plant, which sits under Russian occupation and has generated no electricity since 2022, the facility lost all external power for more than 12 hours on November 8 — its 27th complete loss of off-site power since the invasion — and has spent a cumulative two months without external electricity over the past year, according to Bellona's analysis.
What each side says: Ukraine frames its long-range strikes as degrading the fuel and money that power Russia's war machine, and Zelenskyy has presented the refining campaign as a deliberate strategy. Russia presents its own strikes as hitting energy infrastructure that supports Ukraine's war effort, claims to intercept the overwhelming majority of Ukrainian drones, and says the Kerch Bridge will be rebuilt "even better than before" — though one analyst told reporters it "won't be repaired during this war." The nuclear regulators, for their part, urged Moscow to halt strikes on nuclear facilities and the infrastructure that supplies them, and urged European governments to coordinate emergency preparations.
For ordinary people, the squeeze is now visible on both sides. In Russia, fuel shortages are already appearing in some regions and some areas have reintroduced rationing, according to earlier reporting this month; in Ukraine, civilians in Odesa are being killed in city-centre strikes while Kyiv heads into freezing weather on a few hours of power a day. The nuclear warning adds a new dimension: a grid failure at the wrong moment would not just mean cold homes, but a potential radiological emergency that, as the regulators note, would not respect borders.
In short: Kyiv's drone campaign has now cut Russian oil refining nearly in half by one independent measure, while Russia's retaliation keeps hitting Ukrainian cities and the power grid — and the people who regulate nuclear safety in 38 countries say this winter carries the highest accident risk of the war so far. Watch whether Russia's refining keeps falling, whether the grid holds as temperatures drop, and what, if anything, Thursday's Shenzhen trilateral produces on Ukraine.
Sources:
Source: kwsn.com.

item.title: "Kuwait says Iran attacked it with drones overnight, and Iran says it hit a US base in Kuwait" — Rest of the World Report
item.description:
No new strikes were reported in the Gulf today, but the diplomatic fallout from overnight's attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain kept growing. Kuwait's Foreign Ministry condemned the drone attack as a "flagrant violation of its sovereignty," Bahrain called Iran's attacks on its territory criminal, and the Gulf Cooperation Council, Qatar and the UAE condemned the strikes on both countries. GCC Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi held Iran responsible for the escalation. The Arab League asked the UN Security Council to act. Iran's Revolutionary Guard warned that any use of regional military bases for hostile operations against Iran "will not go unanswered," and Iranian Army chief Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami said his forces were monitoring enemy movements after a third US aircraft carrier arrived in the region. Meanwhile the oil market shrugged: Brent crude traded around $92.50 a barrel on Wednesday, down roughly 0.5–0.7% on the day and about 20% lower for the month, as a 5.3-million-barrel build in US crude inventories and the International Energy Agency's finding that global supply has surpassed demand outweighed the fighting. One analysis notes Brent has fallen about 16% over the month despite the attacks on Kuwait, Bahrain and tankers in the strait.
Sources:
Source: restoftheworldreport.com.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard warned that any use of regional military bases for hostile operations against Iran "will not go unanswered," and Iranian Army chief Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami said his forces were monitoring enemy movements after a third US aircraft carrier arrived in the region. Meanwhile the oil market shrugged: Brent crude traded around $92.50 a barrel on Wednesday, down roughly 0.5–0.7% on the day and about 20% lower for the month, as a 5.3-million-barrel build in US crude inventories and the International Energy Agency's finding that global supply has surpassed demand outweighed the fighting. One analysis notes Brent has fallen about 16% over the month despite the attacks on Kuwait, Bahrain and tankers in the strait.

item.title: "Xi, Trump and Putin gather in Shenzhen for first trilateral summit" — Kilambi News
item.description:
Ahead of Thursday's first-ever trilateral, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin held a bilateral meeting in Shenzhen on Wednesday lasting more than two hours — their fifth meeting this year — and both used their APEC remarks to criticise Western trade protectionism and sanctions, without naming the US directly. The Associated Press reported on Wednesday that Trump will also meet Putin separately on Thursday, in addition to the three-way session — their first face-to-face meeting since the 2025 Alaska summit, which failed to produce a deal on Ukraine. Thursday's schedule, per published reports: an APEC leaders' family photograph at 9:30 a.m. local time, a Trump–Xi bilateral at 12:45 p.m., and the closed-door trilateral at 2:30 p.m. local time, with nuclear arms, Ukraine and Iran on the table. The trilateral's nuclear stakes are sharpened by the expiry of the New START treaty in February 2026, which ended the last formal limits on US and Russian strategic arsenals. Analysts still expect no substantive breakthroughs, and whether a separate Trump–Putin meeting takes place is disputed between reports — Axios says yes, citing a US official; the Kremlin has not confirmed it.
Sources:
Source: news.kilambi.com.

item.title: "Red Sea Shipping Disruption: Conditional Route Return Amid Yemen Escalation" — CrisisBrief
item.description:
Houthi health officials reported 15 people killed and 13 wounded in a coalition strike on a foam factory in Hodeidah, according to a new situation analysis — a casualty claim that has not been independently verified. The strike came during the coalition's campaign against Houthi positions as the group advances toward Aden, reported in this morning's brief. Separately, Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have announced a conditional return of three of their Gemini services to the Suez route from December 2026 or January 2027, the first sign that major carriers may start testing Red Sea transits again despite the Houthi advance on the Bab al-Mandeb approaches — though actual sailings, rather than the announcement, will show whether route avoidance is really easing.

item.title: "Nov 18 Advisory: OpenJDK Remote Code Execution (Java4Shell) [CVE-2026-114938]" — Censys
item.description:
The Java4Shell flaw (CVE-2026-114938) reported in this morning's brief has moved a step closer to real-world exploitation. Censys updated its advisory on Wednesday to note that exploit code is now circulating: public repositories claim, without independent verification, working exploit chains against lab applications, and VulnCheck says a full exploit is available to its customers. The researchers who found the flaw say they are holding back app-specific exploits to give people time to update. As of today there is still no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation and the flaw is not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The researchers demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution against default installs of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and authenticated code execution on Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. Oracle rates it 8.1; the researchers rate it 9.2. If you run Java 17, 21, 25 or 27 on x86-64 servers with AVX-512 VBMI processors, install your vendor's November update — or restart affected JVMs with the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics flag until a fixed build is in place.
Sources:
Source: censys.com.

item.title: "CISA KEV Additions by Date" — East Bay Cyber
item.description:
CISA added four vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Wednesday, November 18: CVE-2024-10441 (Synology DiskStation Manager), CVE-2026-40217 (BerriAI LiteLLM — unprotected alternate channel), CVE-2026-90817 (Vanderbilt REDCap — code injection), and CVE-2026-90436 (Apache Axis — unsafe reflection). The last one is the zero-day behind the N-able N-central compromise reported in last night's brief as single-source and unconfirmed — its KEV listing now confirms it is being exploited in the wild, with 21 servers reported compromised. The catalog now stands at 1,786 entries, with 38 added in the last 30 days. Federal agencies must patch the new entries by their CISA deadlines; everyone else should treat KEV additions as patch-now.
Sources:
Source: eastbaycyber.com.

item.title: "Netanyahu trial prosecutors to cross-examine Mandelblit after defense drops objection" — JBizNews
item.description:
Prosecutors in Benjamin Netanyahu's criminal trial will be allowed to cross-examine former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit after defense lawyers withdrew their objection on Wednesday, easing the restrictions that prompted an unusual prosecution petition to the High Court of Justice this week. The Jerusalem District Court said the arrangement will apply going forward to witnesses called by the defense, whether or not they had originally appeared on the prosecution's witness list — expressly including Mandelblit, whose testimony has focused on his authorization of the investigations into Netanyahu and the indictment. The dispute before the High Court is not fully over: defense lawyers asked for the petition to be struck out and Sunday's hearing canceled, while prosecutors sought clarification of the law, and Supreme Court President Isaac Amit directed the state to say by noon on Thursday whether it is maintaining its petition. Mandelblit's questioning by the defense has not finished — his testimony was interrupted after additional material about his investigation approvals was disclosed to the defense.
Source:
Source: jbiznews.com.

item.title: Open source — November 18
item.description:
A busy release day for developer tools. Microsoft's Visual Studio Code 1.147 shipped today, adding model routers, scheduled agent requests and browser use. OpenCode 2.3.1 and 2.3.2 landed the same day, adding GPT-6.2 support and keeping timed-out commands running. OpenAI's Codex CLI 0.170.0 can now negotiate realtime voice calls in the terminal. Dify 1.20.0, the open-source LLM app platform, now exports traces to any OpenTelemetry collector and keeps Langfuse working after its legacy ingestion change. Mistral Vibe 3.1.3 makes Mistral Large 4 the default model and adds a /goal command. And GitHub put Event Streams — which can wake an agent when a pull request changes — into preview, and made GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol generally available in Copilot. Smaller releases: n8n 2.48.5, Lobe Chat v2.3.4, LiteLLM v1.110.0, Goose v1.60.1 and Phoenix v21.2.0.
Sources:
Source: vibestacklab.com.

item.title: Kyiv is running on four hours of power a day as Russia's grid campaign grinds on
item.description:
Russia launched another 141 long-range drones at Ukraine overnight, and the country's energy minister says Moscow has now hit Ukrainian energy facilities more than 1,000 times since September. In Kyiv, the power crisis has become the war's civilian front line: many homes get electricity for only around four hours a day, some have gone 37 hours straight without it, and the mayor is now in a public fight with the president over who failed to prepare for winter.
Ukraine's Air Force said it intercepted 126 of the 141 drones launched overnight, including 59 jet-powered ones, with impacts recorded at seven locations. Local authorities reported five people killed and 15 wounded across the country over the past day — four in Donetsk region, one in Kharkiv, six injured in Dnipro including a 15-year-old boy, and three more in Sumy. Energy infrastructure was damaged in Kyiv, Mykolaiv and Rivne regions; a strike in Rivne cut power to 80 settlements. President Zelenskyy said the overnight attacks damaged power generation facilities and substations in nine regions, leaving emergency outages in many cities. Russia's Defence Ministry confirmed it hit two power stations in Kyiv and Zhytomyr regions.
The Guardian reports from Kyiv that the outages are now shaping daily life and politics. Residents in the capital are being urged to use public drinking-water fountains, and emergency centres offering hot tea and charging points have been set up in the worst-hit areas. Maksym Bakhmatov, head of Kyiv's Desnianskyi district — home to 600,000 people — blamed the crisis first on Putin and second on Mayor Vitali Klitschko's management, saying the city built no backup generation and has "almost a collapse." Zelenskyy publicly blamed Klitschko last week for failing to prepare for the heating season; Klitschko shot back that the central government was trying to "get rid of Klitschko by any means necessary" and was "in fact destroying Kyiv." About 500 people protested outside City Hall on October 17 demanding the mayor's resignation over winter readiness and shelter shortages.
What each side says: Ukraine and its allies describe a deliberate campaign against civilian energy — the Guardian notes it previously reported on intercepted Russian plans to make Kyiv uninhabitable by cutting electricity, heating, water and even sewage, and the US-based Institute for the Study of War said in a November 7 report that the intercepted plan confirms the systematic nature of the attacks. Russia presents the strikes as hitting energy infrastructure that supports Ukraine's war effort and has not acknowledged targeting civilians. Meanwhile, Ukrainian strikes overnight hit Russian energy infrastructure too, leaving parts of occupied Crimea on outage schedules, according to Russia's Energy Ministry.
For ordinary people, this is now a winter-survival problem, not just a battlefield one. Kyiv is heading into freezing temperatures with a grid that is being hit nightly; Kharkiv's mayor told the Guardian his city faces a "catastrophic" funding shortage for heating and is trying to build decentralised "energy islands" — small fuel-powered generators and modular boilers — but called it "very costly and time-consuming." In Kyiv, Bakhmatov said his district of 600,000 has no workable evacuation plan: "We need help with the generators, with food, with power stations, and so on. Just help us."
In short: Russia's nightly drone campaign is steadily degrading Ukraine's grid — over 1,000 energy strikes since September — and Kyiv is now rationing power to hours a day while its leaders argue over who is to blame. Watch whether the grid holds as temperatures drop, and whether the political fight in Kyiv escalates.
Sources:
Source: zot.news.
