item.title: The US-Iran exchange widens: Qeshm strike answered by drones over Bahrain and Kuwait, tankers still burning
item.description:
The US and Iran traded fire again on Tuesday, and the exchange kept spreading overnight: after American jets hit an Iranian missile site on Qeshm Island, Iran sent drones at US forces in Bahrain and — for the first time in about two and a half months — Kuwait. In the Strait of Hormuz, more tankers caught fire, one crew member is missing, and a third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the Gulf.
A US military official told Reuters and AFP that American fighter jets used precision munitions to strike an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps missile launch site on Qeshm Island, describing it as self-defence in response to Iranian aggression against US personnel and assets. The strike came hours after the IRGC said its drones carried out a "precision operation" against a US-operated radar at Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain — the third Iranian attack on Bahrain in five days. Bahrain said it intercepted the drones with no casualties or damage. Overnight into Wednesday, Bahrain's defence force said it intercepted a further round of Iranian aerial attacks, and Kuwait's military said its air defences were responding to hostile drone attacks around 1:39 a.m. Gulf time. Iran's army then said its drones had targeted Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Ali Al-Salem Air Base in Kuwait. Kuwait has not named the origin of the drones and reported no casualties or damage.
At sea, the IRGC navy claimed two "violating" vessels — a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude and an LNG carrier — exploded and caught fire after hitting naval mines, and warned ships using the southern route faced "a wall of iron and fire" of mines. Independent trackers reported a third vessel hit, and Iran's army separately reported a fourth tanker damaged east of the strait. None of the mine claims has been independently verified, and the US military says it has cleared the main routes. What is confirmed: the Panama-flagged LPG carrier Tara Gas was struck twice off Oman, suffering an engine-room fire; India's shipping minister said 24 crew were accounted for but one Indian sailor is missing. The Panama-flagged On Phoenix was also hit by an unknown projectile off Oman on Monday. Region Alert, citing ADNOC, reported an ADNOC Logistics vessel was attacked on November 17 with 11 crew injured and one missing at sea. The USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the region on Monday, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington — three US carrier strike groups near Iran.
What each side says: Washington describes its strikes along Iran's southern coast as limited and defensive, and CNN noted the Qeshm strike resembled others US officials have also called defensive rather than a significant escalation. Tehran says its drone attacks answer repeated US drone violations of Iranian airspace, and its foreign ministry has rejected as "rubbish" a CNN report — citing seven US officials — that Iran is developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials in Washington with a dirty bomb or chemical weapon; the White House says there are no credible threats to the homeland. Trump has said further strikes on Iran are "quite unlikely" and the military part of the war is "effectively over." Diplomacy is still running in parallel: Qatar's foreign ministry says mediation continues after a meeting with the Iranian side on Tuesday, and Iran's foreign minister met Oman's foreign minister and Sultan Haitham in Muscat to discuss maritime corridors and preventing escalation.
For ordinary people, the costs are stacking up in the strait and at the pump. Brent crude was around $92.76 a barrel on Wednesday morning per Reuters — up slightly on the day but well below April's wartime peak of $126.41 — while shipping through the strait, which carried about a fifth of the world's traded oil and gas in peacetime, remains partly blocked and heavily escorted. Seafarers are paying the sharpest price: one crew member missing from the Tara Gas, another reported missing from an ADNOC vessel, and crews evacuating burning ships. Iraq has resumed pumping oil to Turkey by pipeline at 120,000 barrels a day, rising to 500,000, to avoid Hormuz altogether.
In short: the tit-for-tat is no longer confined to one country — US strikes on Qeshm drew Iranian drone attacks on both Bahrain and Kuwait, tankers keep burning in the strait, and three US carriers are now in the region. Watch whether Kuwait confirms and attributes the overnight drone attack, whether US Central Command details the Qeshm strike, and whether Thursday's Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral produces any pressure to step back.
Caption: A day-264 graphic from The Atlantic Digest's running coverage of the US-Iran war, which entered its ninth month after US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28. The graphic marks the day US jets hit Qeshm Island and Iran's drones reached Bahrain and Kuwait.
Sources:
Source: atlanticdigest.com.

item.title: Coalition hits 60 Houthi targets as the Houthis close on Aden — and Yemen's government brands them terrorists
item.description:
The Saudi-led coalition carried out a "precision operation" against 60 Houthi military targets on Tuesday, as the Houthis press their advance toward Aden and Yemen's internationally recognised government formally designated the group a terrorist organisation.
Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said on Wednesday morning that the strikes hit Sanaa, Hodeidah, Amran and Saada governorates and destroyed tunnels the Houthis used as workshops and storage for ballistic missiles. The operation came during the Houthis' advance toward Aden, the government's temporary capital, after government-aligned forces withdrew from Dhubab airport and territory around the Bab al-Mandeb strait to defend the city. The Houthis are now reported to be about 60 kilometres from Aden. The coalition also said it intercepted two Houthi cruise missiles launched toward Riyadh on Wednesday; the Houthis' military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group targeted oil pumping stations near Riyadh and a radar installation in southern Saudi Arabia, which Saudi authorities have not confirmed. Alerts sounded in Jizan, Najran and Khamis Mushait on Wednesday before the danger passed.
In Taiz, fighting has resumed in Tur al-Bahah in Lahij province, and Al Jazeera's correspondent there reports "fierce battles" between government forces and the Houthis. Local authorities accuse the Houthis of shelling civilians and residential neighbourhoods; villages in Jabal Sabr are described as under complete siege, with daily sniper attacks targeting civilians, primarily children and women. Taiz authorities also accuse the Houthis of blocking medicine shipments coming from Aden and confiscating medical supplies, and have called on the United Nations to intervene, saying the blockade endangers "the lives of thousands of patients." Separately, Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council chairman issued Law 1/2026, published by the SABA news agency on November 18, designating the Houthis a terrorist organisation, with criminal provisions and restrictions on financing.
What each side says: the coalition frames its strikes as precision attacks on Houthi missile capability, and the Yemeni army claims hundreds of operations against Houthi positions. The Houthis present their attacks as strikes on Saudi military, civilian and oil infrastructure, and say the Bab al-Mandeb shipping lanes are "safer now" in their hands. The advance has also revived Yemen's southern separatists: STC leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi has launched a mobilisation campaign to defend Aden, Lahij and al-Dhalea, and one STC representative told Al Jazeera that "in January, the most effective anti-Houthi force in Yemen was taken apart by decisions in Riyadh, not by the Houthis" — a reference to the Saudi-backed campaign that weakened the separatists earlier this year. Analysts are split on whether the STC can hold Aden, with one expert warning Houthi capabilities exceed those of the government and the STC combined.
For ordinary people, the squeeze is worst in Taiz, where a siege is cutting off medicine as well as movement, and in the south, where the International Organization for Migration counts 348,000 people displaced since August 1 as the front line moves toward Aden. If the Houthis take the Bab al-Mandeb coast in force, shipping through the strait — normally about 12% of global trade — faces a new threat, and Saudi Arabia's overland oil alternative, the East-West Pipeline to Yanbu, has already been hit by drones before.
In short: the coalition is hitting back hard — 60 targets in a day — but the Houthis are still advancing on Aden, Yemen's government has now formally labelled them terrorists, and Taiz is under siege with medicine blocked. Watch whether the Houthis push the last 60 kilometres to Aden and whether the STC's mobilisation holds the southern front.

Source: barbadosgazette.com.

item.title: Nvidia's first earnings without Huang were a blowout — and the stock still can't shake the scandal
item.description:
Nvidia's first quarterly report since Jensen Huang resigned blew past Wall Street's expectations, and the board used the earnings call to rule out his return and announce a $150 billion share buyback. The shares jumped about 5% after hours and were up roughly 3% before Wednesday's open — but they remain about 35% below their October record, and the market's reaction was notably cooler than the numbers.
Revenue for the quarter ended October 25 was $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier and well above the roughly $109.1 billion analysts expected, with adjusted earnings of $2.68 a share against forecasts of about $2.47. Data centre revenue hit $107.6 billion, up 110% year over year, and net income reached $65.3 billion. Guidance for the current quarter was $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, ahead of the roughly $125.1 billion consensus, and interim CEO Colette Kress raised the fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to about 75% from 70%. Kress said the new Vera Rubin platform generated "nearly $20 billion" in its first quarter of production shipments — the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history, according to the company. The board also approved an additional $150 billion in share repurchases, bringing total remaining buyback capacity to $227.3 billion, after returning $28.1 billion to shareholders in the quarter.
The leadership question dominated the call as much as the numbers. Board chair Harvey Jones opened by saying the board "unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," and declined to take questions about the internal investigation. Jones said Huang resigned after disclosing personal conduct "inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms." The board has hired Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent CEO and created a board committee on national security and export control oversight. Huang said on Tuesday he would be "honoured" to return if the board judged it in shareholders' interest, and said "I own my mistakes completely." He is due to appear before congressional committees on December 1, followed by Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter on December 2, according to AP. Meanwhile Washington tightened the screws further: the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule on Monday requiring data centre operators in Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand to get a US government licence before exporting advanced AI chips — aimed at stopping Nvidia chips being rented to Chinese companies through overseas data centres. Nvidia earned $2.4 billion from licensed chip sales to China in the quarter and has now ceased those shipments.
What each side says: bulls point to the numbers — demand held up without Huang, guidance went up, and one analyst told CNN the results show "an orderly CEO transition does not necessarily have to dilute the company's value." The sceptics note the stock is still down about 17% for the year and roughly $2 trillion of market value has been erased since the October 6 record of $243.37, and as one fund manager told Reuters, "the story here is very complicated, and it's hard not to factor that in as an additional risk." Gross margin is also set to narrow to 71–72% in the current quarter from 74.8%, as the newest products ramp.
For ordinary people, this is the bellwether for the whole AI trade: Nvidia's stock had its sixth straight weekly decline heading into the report, its longest losing streak, and the Nasdaq fell into correction on Monday. A clean beat that only buys a 3–5% bounce tells investors the market is pricing the unresolved scandal, not just the chips. The next test comes tonight, when Anthropic prices its IPO ahead of Thursday's Nasdaq debut.
In short: Nvidia proved the business still works without Huang — $115.8 billion in revenue, a raised outlook and a $150 billion buyback — but the board has closed the door on his return, Washington is tightening chip curbs, and the stock is still roughly a third below its peak. Watch Wednesday's regular session for whether the bounce holds, and Huang's congressional appearance on December 1.
Caption: Nvidia's share price chart and branding from Wealth Professional's report on the earnings beat — the stock gained roughly 5% in after-hours trading on Tuesday after revenue of $115.8 billion, but remains about 35% below its October record high.
Sources:
Source: cdn-res.keymedia.com.

item.title: Trump lands in Shenzhen for a first-ever trilateral with Xi and Putin
item.description:
Donald Trump met Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in Manila on Wednesday, announced a new Philippines trade deal, and then flew to Shenzhen, where China's Xi Jinping greeted him on the tarmac — a rare honour Xi did not extend to Vladimir Putin when he arrived earlier in the day. On Thursday, the three leaders hold the first-ever US-China-Russia trilateral, with nuclear arms, Ukraine and Iran on the agenda.
Trump's Asia trip opened on Tuesday with the first Quad meeting in two years — Trump, India's Narendra Modi, Japan's Sanae Takaichi and Australia's Anthony Albanese — which produced a joint statement expressing "grave concerns" about economic coercion, including through arbitrary export restrictions, without naming China. The statement also flagged joint maritime patrol-aircraft exercises next year and an AI accelerator with more than $85 million in funding. Trump then met Marcos at Malacañang Palace on Wednesday, had lunch, and announced a new trade deal — though he had also said last year that an agreement had been reached, and no details were given beyond the White House saying Manila will buy more energy and farm products. The US goods deficit with the Philippines has risen from $4.9 billion in 2024 to $12.8 billion in the first nine months of this year, according to the Census Bureau. Trump also signed a trade deal with Thailand on Tuesday under which Bangkok will eliminate tariffs on US exports. In Shenzhen, Xi greeted Trump at the foot of Air Force One's stairs with a handshake that became a hug, as dancers waved flowers and flags — reciprocating a gesture Trump made during Xi's state visit to Washington in September.
What each side says: Trump says he plans to use Thursday's trilateral to talk about limiting nuclear weapons and ending the war in Ukraine, saying "I think it's very close to getting it done," and he has teased a private meeting with Putin and a separate sit-down with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that Trump was "serious" about meeting Kim, but that no meeting was currently scheduled for Thursday. Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting, and Trump's own aides had told reporters before the trip that Ukraine would not be on the agenda. China, for its part, has accused the US of "economic coercion" over its latest restrictions on Chinese access to advanced chips, and has effectively shut off exports of key critical minerals to Japan for nearly a year as relations between Asia's two largest economies have nosedived.
For ordinary people, the backdrop is a trade truce that expires in January and a chip war that is already reshaping supply chains — Washington's new rules on renting advanced AI chips through overseas data centres landed on Monday, just as Trump arrived in Asia. At home, a run of technical outages at Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase and the NSA's communications network overshadowed the trip; Rubio stepped in to reassure Americans, saying there was "zero" evidence the outages are connected or tied to rival nations, hackers or criminals, and that they stemmed from systems being fixed after vulnerabilities were found. In Manila, demonstrators gathered for a fifth day of protests that included burning Trump effigies and calls to end the Middle East war.
In short: Trump arrives in Shenzhen with a Philippines trade deal in hand and a tarmac welcome from Xi, but Thursday's trilateral — the first time the leaders of the US, China and Russia have met three-way — is where the substance is supposed to happen, on nuclear arms, Ukraine and Iran. Watch Thursday at 2:30 p.m. local time, and whether anything concrete comes out of it.
Sources:
Source: thehindubusinessline.com.

item.title: "Java flaw leaves systems open to hackers, say US, South Korea, China's Tencent" — Reuters
item.description:
The Java4Shell flaw (CVE-2026-114938) reported last night is now drawing urgent government warnings. Reuters reports US and South Korean authorities and China's Tencent have urged companies to patch the critical flaw in Java's Base64 decoder, which can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on systems with AVX-512 VBMI processors. South Korea's presidential office held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, and its science ministry and internet security agency said on Wednesday that public institutions and private enterprises must urgently install the updates. Tencent Cloud warned customers the flaw — dubbed "Java4Shell" — could let unauthenticated attackers steal sensitive information or take control of affected servers. CISA has urged immediate patching, internet-facing systems first; Oracle shipped fixed builds on November 17. No known exploitation as of last night.
Source:
Source: kwsn.com.

item.title: "Attackers Compromise Microsoft's Agent Framework PyPI Package to Steal Cloud Credentials" — The Hacker News
item.description:
Two malicious versions of Microsoft's agent-framework Python package (1.26.1 and 1.26.2) were published to PyPI 33 minutes apart on Tuesday evening, carrying a credential stealer that runs every time Python starts — even if the package is never imported — by dropping a .pth startup file. The stealer targets Azure and Azure DevOps credentials, environment variables with names containing TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD or KEY, credential files (.azure, .npmrc, .netrc, .git-credentials, Docker config, Hugging Face tokens), and in the second version, GitHub Actions OIDC tokens. Both versions were removed within about 45 minutes, and the last safe version is 1.26.0. Wiz, which reported it to Microsoft, says the attacker appears to have used a compromised client certificate and private key for Microsoft's internal release-signing pipeline; SafeDep found PyPI now lists a second maintainer, "vibiret," an account created on the day of the attack. The package gets about 190,000 downloads a month, so any CI pipeline that installed it in that window should pin agent-framework==1.26.0, rebuild, and rotate every secret it could have touched.
Sources:
Source: wiz.io.

item.title: "Anthropic Set to Price IPO Tonight, Reports Point Above $80" — Invezz
item.description:
Anthropic is due to set its IPO price tonight after the US market close, with shares starting trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT. The official range in its November 17 SEC filing is still $70–$78 a share for 825 million shares, but the Wall Street Journal and CNBC report it is likely to price above $80 on strong demand — Bloomberg reports orders of nearly seven times the shares available. At $78 the offering would raise $64.35 billion; a separate $26 billion private placement to seven strategic investors (Google, Microsoft, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, TSMC) closes at the same price. Up to 20% of the offering is allocated to retail investors.
Sources:
Source: invezz.com.

item.title: Open source — November 18
item.description:
GitHub's trending board reshuffled overnight with one big change at the top: elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter — an 82-skill bug-hunting and red-team bundle for Claude Code built from 681 disclosed vulnerability reports — is now number one, at 10,113 stars and gaining about 1,005 a day. Two of the oldest names in agent tooling are back on the board past 300,000 stars each: obra/superpowers (319,614 stars, +1,917/day), a skills framework and development methodology for coding agents, and affaan-m/ECC (305,910 stars, +883/day), a harness-optimisation system for several coding agents. jingyaogong/minimind (66,332 stars) is trending again with a 64M-parameter language model it says can be trained from scratch in about two hours. New risers: google-research/paper-orchestra (~3,007 stars, +1,072/day), a Google framework that turns research notes into papers; gylive/google-ultra (+2,565/day); krisgfx9/Wireless-Device-Battery-Monitor (+2,693/day), a tray app showing the battery level of wireless mice, headsets, keyboards and controllers on Windows; and erkamyaman/rust-anything (+2,291/day), a tool for rewriting an app in Rust piece by piece, checked against the original's recorded behaviour. dream-num/univer keeps climbing (29,673 stars, +1,774/day).
Sources:
Source: medium.com.

item.title: US strikes Qeshm after Iran hits Bahrain — and the war spreads to Kuwait
item.description:
The United States confirmed on Tuesday that its fighter jets struck an Iranian missile site on Qeshm Island, after Iran targeted a US radar in Bahrain for the third time in five days — and the day's fighting spread further, with Kuwait saying it faced hostile drone attacks and Bahrain intercepting more Iranian drones overnight. It is the sharpest single-day escalation in the Gulf war in weeks, and it came even as Qatari mediators kept meeting Iranian officials.
The details, as reported by Reuters, AP, CBS and Iranian state media: a US military official, speaking anonymously, said US fighter jets fired on a Revolutionary Guards missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, calling the strike "self-defense" and "in response to IRGC aggression targeting US personnel and assets." Hours earlier, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they had targeted a US radar system at Bahrain's Sheikh Isa base; Bahrain and US Central Command said the drones were intercepted, with no casualties or damage. It was the third attempted Iranian strike on a US military installation in five days, and all three were intercepted, US officials said. Iranian media reported five or six explosions on Qeshm on Tuesday afternoon, and Hormozgan deputy governor Ahmad Nafisi said the strikes caused no damage to residential, commercial or infrastructure areas. AP notes the strikes broke a lull of about two months, though limited US strikes on Qeshm have continued periodically. Overnight, Bahrain's defence force said it had intercepted more Iranian aerial attacks on Wednesday, and Kuwait's military said on Tuesday evening it was hitting back at "hostile drone attacks," with air defences intercepting them — no one has claimed responsibility for the Kuwait attack.
Iran, meanwhile, made a string of claims that have not been independently verified: its Revolutionary Guards said they shot down a US MQ-1 Predator south of Qeshm at about 1:45 p.m., calling it the 18th MQ-1 they claim to have downed, and the army separately said it downed a US-made LUCAS drone over the strait. Iran's navy said a supertanker and an LPG carrier caught fire after striking mines, one reportedly carrying two million barrels of crude, and a third tanker was later reported on fire. The US has not confirmed either drone loss — Washington rarely confirms or denies individual drone losses — and Reuters could not independently verify the tanker claims. What is confirmed independently is that UK Maritime Trade Operations said the crew of a tanker attacked north of the Omani port of Khasab was unaccounted for, and shipping monitors counted 17 confirmed incidents in the strait this month. Iran's navy warned shipping firms against using the southern route, calling it "an iron and fiery wall of mines," while the US military said in late October it had cleared the strait's main transit routes.
The two sides are also fighting a war of words over something darker. CNN reported, citing US intelligence assessments, that Iran could be developing plans to target administration officials with a dirty bomb or chemical weapon in Washington — the reporting stressed it was "an effort to give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack." Trump said the US takes it very seriously and that Iran would "pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before" if it set off a dirty bomb in Washington. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, called the reports "RUBBISH" and invoked the false Iraq WMD claims of 2003: "Spare us the Iraq War-style propaganda." The New York Times separately reported that Iran's network of dams might be cover for underground missile development. On diplomacy, Qatar's foreign ministry said mediation continues and a meeting with the Iranian side was held on Tuesday, warning that escalation poses an "extremely grave danger" to reaching an agreement; Araghchi also met Oman's foreign minister and Sultan Haitham in Muscat, where the two sides discussed safeguarding maritime corridors.
For ordinary people, the cost is showing up in fuel prices and in the risks borne by seafarers. Brent crude settled at $93.14 a barrel on Tuesday, up 0.76%, and WTI at $86.01 — well below April's wartime peak of $126.41, but the market swung all day on each new incident, and Brent eased to about $92.98 on Wednesday morning after US inventory data showed a 5.28-million-barrel build. Iraq resumed pumping oil to Turkey through its pipeline at 120,000 barrels a day, rising toward 500,000, specifically to avoid the strait. Inside Iran, Amnesty International said on Tuesday that the authorities have used the cover of war to intensify repression after the January crackdown, with its lead researcher saying "there is no doubt that thousands were massacred in less than 48 hours" — the exact toll still cannot be quantified after the January 8–9 internet blackout.
In short: the US confirmed it hit an IRGC missile site on Qeshm in self-defense after Iran's third attack on Bahrain in five days, Iran claims two US drones downed and three more tankers hit by mines — none of it verified — and the fighting spread to Kuwait, with Bahrain intercepting more drones overnight. Watch whether Washington confirms or denies the drone losses, whether the tanker attacks continue, and Thursday's Shenzhen trilateral, where Trump says he will raise Iran.
Sources:
Source: jurnal.jumanji.workers.dev.

item.title: Another night of strikes on the grids — and the Kerch arch is in the sea
item.description:
Russia hit Ukraine's power grid again overnight, Ukraine struck back at Russian energy sites, and the full scale of Ukraine's Kerch Bridge attack is now clear: Reuters-verified video shows the bridge's main road arch has crumbled into the sea. Britain, meanwhile, announced more than 1,000 new air-defence missiles for Ukraine's winter, and a Russian drone flew over Moldova's capital.
The details, as reported by Al Jazeera and Reuters: Zelensky said Russia's overnight attacks damaged power generation facilities and substations in nine regions, leaving emergency outages in many cities, with hours-long power and water outages across Kyiv and surrounding regions. Russia's Defence Ministry said it hit two power stations in the Kyiv and Zhytomyr regions, and Reuters, citing Ukraine's emergency service, reported strikes on Poltava, Dnipro, Kirovohrad and Rivne as well. On the other side, Ukrainian drone strikes killed three people in Russia's Belgorod region, according to local Russian authorities, and Russia's Energy Ministry said Ukrainian strikes hit energy infrastructure overnight, with temporary outage schedules in force and parts of Russian-occupied Crimea also losing power. Russia claimed it downed 709 Ukrainian drones across 14 regions, Crimea and the Black and Azov seas — a figure that, like all such tallies, has not been independently verified.
On the Kerch Bridge, the picture sharpened on Tuesday. Videos and images posted by Zelensky and verified by Reuters showed the bridge's main road arch had crumbled into the sea, leaving a yawning gap after two strikes in as many days. Crimea's Moscow-installed governor, Sergei Aksyonov, said two people were killed and road traffic was suspended, with rail traffic partially resumed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov promised a repair plan that would make the bridge "even better than before," but Russian military bloggers and other experts said repairs would be hard given Ukraine's capacity to strike again, and Finnish military analyst Emil Kastehelmi posted: "The road bridge won't be repaired during this war." Zelensky framed the operation as payback — "Russia strikes our infrastructure every day, including bridges... we are reminding Russia that war will always return to where it began" — and said Ukraine had repeatedly offered de-escalation steps that Russia rejected. In Moldova, President Maia Sandu said a Russian drone flew over the capital Chisinau, a rare occurrence, and pledged to press for further sanctions; Russia rejected the accusation, saying no proof had been provided.
The allies' answer to the winter campaign came at the Ukraine Defence Contact Group in Brussels. Britain announced a £240 million package — more than 1,000 additional short-range air-defence missiles and launchers, plus more than a dozen air-defence radars — with deliveries starting in mid-December, on top of 400 surface-to-air missiles already supplied ahead of winter. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the systems, built by Thales in Belfast, have proven effective against the Iranian-designed jet-powered Shahed drones Russia is using against Ukrainian cities. The package is part of a £500 million pledge from last month's Budget, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham is expected to announce the remaining support at a "coalition of the willing" meeting on Thursday. Germany and Britain also rejected Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby's criticism of Ukraine's deep strikes at the Brussels meeting: Pistorius called the nightly Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy, water and heating infrastructure "kind of terrorism," and Streeting said Ukraine's strikes "helped to degrade Putin's war machine, buying time and saving lives."
For ordinary people, it is the power grid that decides the winter. About 700,000 households in the Dnipropetrovsk region were without electricity on Tuesday morning, and the new overnight strikes hit nine more regions' generation and substations. In Kyiv, the two struck bridges are still only partly reopened, and some districts remain on backup heating. The human toll keeps rising from earlier strikes too: Ukraine's national police said the death toll from the November 2 Russian strike on a humanitarian aid centre in the frontline village of Komyshuvakha has risen to 72, with four people still missing.
In short: both sides spent another night hitting each other's energy infrastructure, the Kerch Bridge's main road arch is now in the sea after two strikes, and Britain pledged 1,000+ missiles and radars for the winter — while a Russian drone over Chisinau rattled Moldova. Watch Thursday's Shenzhen trilateral and whether the overnight grid attacks keep escalating.
Sources:
Source: helsinkitimes.com.

item.title: Quad meets in Manila for the first time in two years — five initiatives, and a warning on economic coercion:
item.description:
Trump, Modi, Japan's Sanae Takaichi and Australia's Anthony Albanese held the 7th Quad Leaders' Summit in Manila on Tuesday, the first in two years and the first of Trump's second term.
The joint statement announced five outcomes — a Quad Business Leaders' Forum in Mumbai in early 2027, counterterrorism cooperation, an Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration, a partnership on cable connectivity and resilience, and enhanced cyber cooperation — plus a Super Intelligence Accelerator backed by more than $85 million for trusted AI access across the region. The leaders said they "strongly oppose" destabilising or unilateral actions that seek to change the status quo "including by force or coercion," and expressed "grave concerns about economic coercion, including through arbitrary export restrictions."
P-8 and P-3C patrol aircraft are due to fly a joint maritime exercise in 2027, the first in a Quad setting. Modi and Trump held no separate bilateral meeting.
(The Hindu BusinessLine · New Kerala / ANI · Astig.ph)
Source: thehindubusinessline.com.

The leaders said they "strongly oppose" destabilising or unilateral actions that seek to change the status quo "including by force or coercion," and expressed "grave concerns about economic coercion, including through arbitrary export restrictions."

item.title: Houthis claim drone hits on two Saudi East-West pipeline pumping stations:
item.description:
the Houthis said on Tuesday they launched five drones at Pumping Station No. 9 west of Riyadh (three drones, in two phases) and Pumping Station No. 8 (two drones), claiming "precise and direct" hits.
The Saudi-led coalition said it shot down a Houthi drone near Riyadh on Tuesday — the fourth straight day of Houthi drone fire into Saudi Arabia, all intercepted, according to the coalition — and there was no Saudi confirmation of pipeline damage. The 750-mile pipeline, with 11 pumping stations and capacity of up to 7 million barrels a day, is Saudi Arabia's bypass around Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb; it was previously knocked out for nearly two weeks by a drone attack on September 11.
The Houthis also said Bab el-Mandeb's shipping lanes are "safer now" in their hands. (CBS live updates · Reuters via SRN News)
Source: jurnal.jumanji.workers.dev.

item.title: Yemen — no change of control around Aden, but the fighting goes on:
item.description:
Saudi aircraft hit Sanaa again on Tuesday, destroying a shoe and textile factory in the Nahda district and wounding nine people, according to Houthi sources; Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said Sanaa, Saada, Taiz, Lahj, al-Jawf and Marib took raids over 24 hours, with clashes continuing in Lahj and Marib and no change of control anywhere.
Saudi Arabia also deported senior Southern Transitional Council leaders to Aden on Tuesday after roughly ten months in detention. And the UN Security Council voted unanimously to extend its Yemen sanctions for one more year, including asset freezes and travel bans.
(The Levant Files · Al Jazeera)
Source: thelevantfiles.org.

item.title: Iraqi militia warns it will fight government forces entering its stronghold:
item.description:
Kataib Hezbollah, a powerful Iran-backed armed group, vowed on Tuesday to confront Iraqi government forces if they try to enter its main stronghold of Jurf al-Sakhar, south of Baghdad — the first major test of new Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's push to disarm non-state armed groups by mid-2027.
Al-Zaidi said security forces would enter later this week, and the group has reportedly been given until Friday to leave. (CBS live updates)
Source: jurnal.jumanji.workers.dev.

item.title: Apple outage — it lasted longer than first reported:
item.description:
Apple's own status page puts iCloud Account & Sign In down from 8:45 a.m. to 1:15 p.m.
PT — four and a half hours, nearly three times the 93 minutes iCloud was down on November 10 — with the App Store down 8:45 a.m. to noon PT and AppleCare on Device 8:15 a.m. to 12:39 p.m. PT.
Downdetector recorded about 2,300 user reports for Apple Pay around 12:20 p.m. ET and about 1,800 for iCloud near its peak.
Apple blames an unspecified internal update, not a cyberattack. (Appdook · ASX News / Reuters)
Source: appdook.com.

item.title: Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching — "Java4Shell" (CVE-2026-114938):
item.description:
a critical memory-corruption flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder can let an unauthenticated attacker crash the JVM or run code remotely.
Security firm Calif, which found the flaw with help from an AI coding tool, rates it 9.2 under CVSS 4.0 (Oracle rates it 8.1); researchers demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution on default installations of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and authenticated RCE on Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. It affects unpatched OpenJDK builds from 17.0.6 onward (branches 17, 21, 25, 27) running on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI — Intel Xeon from Ice Lake through Granite Rapids and AMD EPYC from Zen 4 onward; ARM64 is not affected.
Oracle released fixed builds on November 17 (17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1), and a single JVM flag closes the exposure where patching has to wait. CISA issued an alert on November 17 urging immediate patching, internet-facing systems first, and warning that bundled runtimes in containers and appliances must be found.
No active exploitation has been reported as of November 17. (CISA · Qualys · Sophos)
Source: cisa.gov.

item.title: Norway's Equinor detects ongoing cyberattack, oil and gas output unaffected:
item.description:
Europe's largest gas supplier said on Tuesday it had detected an ongoing cyberattack against some of its IT systems, with its internal email system down and disruptions to IT applications.
The company said it has taken steps to neutralise the attack, that there is no indication data was stolen, and that operations and production are unaffected. Norway's National Security Authority said it is aware of the incident; Norway raised its cyber-risk level to 4 out of 5 in late October.
(Reuters via KWSN · Cryptopolitan)
Source: kwsn.com.

item.title: Optimizely supply-chain attack hit 178 organizations' websites — "OPTIMJACK":
item.description:
Optimizely confirmed that an attacker exploited a flaw in its Web Experimentation account signup flow to inject malicious JavaScript into customer projects, which was then served from Optimizely's own CDN to visitors of at least 178 organizations — including Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock.
The payload swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and delivered iOS exploit kits to iPhone and iPad visitors; about $7,000 in crypto reached the attacker's wallets. Security firm Report URI found the code in 188 of 1,611 snippets it checked, starting with the BBC's snippet at 04:21 UTC on November 16; most of it was cleaned up within a day.
Optimizely says it has fixed the flaw, removed the injected code and secured affected accounts; Salesforce confirmed it was impacted and disabled Optimizely scripts, and Ledger confirmed it was affected. No CVE has been assigned yet, and how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated projects is still unexplained.
(Computerworld · Breach News · Report URI via matt.security)
Source: computerworld.com.

item.title: Netanyahu trial — High Court to hear prosecution bid to cross-examine Mandelblit:
item.description:
Israel's High Court of Justice will hear on Sunday the prosecution's challenge to limits on its questioning of former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit in Netanyahu's criminal trial.
The court issued a conditional order on Tuesday, with responses due Sunday at 10 a.m. ahead of a 3 p.m. hearing before Supreme Court President Isaac Amit and Justices Yael Willner and Khaled Kabub, but declined to suspend the District Court's restrictions in the meantime. The prosecution is challenging the November 2 decision to limit its questioning of Mandelblit — called by the defense about his authorization of the investigations — to re-examination rather than cross-examination.
Separately, Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara's appearance before the trial panel, set for Wednesday, was postponed by a week to November 25. Mandelblit's testimony itself resumes Wednesday, November 18.
(jbiznews)
Source: jbiznews.com.

item.title: Allies split over Ukraine's deep strikes as Germany funds more Patriots
item.description:
The 37th Ramstein meeting in Brussels on Tuesday delivered new air-defence money for Ukraine — and the sharpest public disagreement yet between Washington and its European allies over how Ukraine fights the war. Germany and Norway will jointly finance another PURL package of US weapons for Ukraine, with Germany putting in $300 million, its fifth package, focused on PAC-2 and PAC-3 Patriot missiles. But the meeting's dominant argument was over Ukraine's long-range strikes on Russian territory, with Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby calling them ineffective and Germany's Boris Pistorius and the UK's Wes Streeting publicly pushing back.
The details, as reported by Reuters, Devdiscourse and Ukrainian outlets: Pistorius announced the package ahead of the meeting, saying the focus is air defence, "especially PAC-2 and PAC-3 Patriot missiles," plus IRIS-T systems, radars, F-16 ammunition and drones. He also said Germany is working to integrate its IRIS-T missile with Norwegian NASAMS systems. "Supporting Ukraine is not a charity event… it's about the security of Europe, and it's about stopping Vladimir Putin and putting him in his place," Pistorius said, and he appealed to allies such as Greece that still hold large Patriot stocks. President Volodymyr Zelensky used the meeting to propose a swap: partners would hand over available Patriot and IRIS-T interceptors from their own stocks now, in exchange for newer missiles from Ukraine's existing orders, to close the gap while deliveries lag. Sweden's Defence Minister Pol Johnson said Ukraine needs another 18–24 months to build its own anti-ballistic capability and is preparing to test its FREYJA system this winter. Ukrainian outlets also reported a letter on Gripen fighter jets signed by Ukraine, Sweden and the UK, though that has not been confirmed by the governments involved. Allies also discussed Washington's review of US troop levels in Europe with Colby; Pistorius said to expect changes but nothing concrete yet, with the review's result due before Christmas. Germany hosts about 35,000 US troops, the largest American presence in Europe, and European military sources have speculated Washington could move a brigade — roughly 5,000 troops — from Germany either to Asia or closer to NATO's eastern flank in Poland.
The two sides are arguing about what actually wins this war. Colby, opening the session, praised Ukraine's battlefield gains — he said Ukraine has for a second consecutive month liberated more territory than Russia has captured, and that Russian forces have suffered their heaviest monthly losses of the full-scale war — but judged Ukrainian long-range strikes on Russian civilian infrastructure, including Wildberries warehouses, ineffective for ending the war or slowing the Russian advance, and said US support should focus on holding the front line. He stressed his warnings do not mean Ukraine should fight with its hands tied. Pistorius and Streeting rejected that criticism, arguing that strikes on strategic targets have weakened Russia's war machine. Zelensky's position is that air defence is now Ukraine's chief priority: Patriot stocks are depleted, deliveries are slow, and Russia's ballistic missiles are the one weapon Ukraine cannot reliably stop any other way — which is why he is offering to trade future orders for interceptors sitting in allied depots today.
For ordinary people, the argument lands in the middle of the hardest winter of the war. Russia has hit Ukrainian energy and transport infrastructure daily for weeks, and the overnight strikes on Kyiv's two main bridges (covered in this morning's brief) left parts of the capital without power, water and heating. Kyiv partly reopened both bridges on Tuesday — trams and trolleybuses are back on regular routes, and the Southern Bridge is open to limited one-way traffic — but the Northern Bridge is still closed and the metro's Green Line is still split between the riverbanks. Sweden's warning that Ukraine is 18–24 months from its own anti-ballistic capability is a measure of how long Kyiv will depend on allies for exactly the missiles Colby's critics are arguing about.
In short: Ramstein produced $300 million more for Patriot missiles from Germany and Norway, but exposed a real split — Washington questioning Ukraine's deep strikes on Russian civilian targets, Berlin and London defending them, and Zelensky offering to swap future missile orders for interceptors now. Watch whether any ally actually hands over stockpiled Patriots, and what Colby's troop review says before Christmas.
Sources:
Source: devdiscourse.com.

item.title: Fourth tanker burns in Hormuz as Muscat talks end with no deal — and fresh strikes are reported on Qeshm Island
item.description:
The Gulf war kept escalating on Tuesday even as the diplomats met. A fourth tanker caught fire in or near the Strait of Hormuz in less than 24 hours, Iran said it struck a US radar in Bahrain for the third time in under a week, and Iranian media reported US strikes on Qeshm Island — while talks between Iran's foreign minister and his Omani counterpart in Muscat ended with no agreement and no announcement about negotiations with Washington.
The details, as reported by Terra World News, Traders Union, the Financial Times and others: Iran's navy said a tanker caught fire after hitting a mine on Tuesday, the fourth such incident since Sunday, saying the vessel had been sailing through a restricted zone without coordination and with its navigation systems off. It did not identify the ship, its flag or the crew's condition, and the claim has not been independently verified. Separately, UK Maritime Trade Operations said the UAE-owned LPG tanker Tara Gas was struck twice off the Omani coast on Monday night, the second strike causing a fire on board, with heat-map data showing an explosion near the vessel at about 7 a.m. UK time on Tuesday. UKMTO says at least nine vessels have been attacked in and around the strait in the past 10 days, most near the Omani coast. Iran also said it launched a drone strike against a US air-defence radar system in Bahrain early on Tuesday; Bahraini authorities say they intercepted several Iranian drones targeting the kingdom, home to the US Navy's Fifth Fleet. The Revolutionary Guard said the attack was a response to what it called a violation of Iranian airspace by US drones. Then, on Tuesday afternoon, Iran's semi-official Mehr news agency reported US strikes on several locations on Qeshm Island in the strait, and Israel's Channel 12, citing unofficial sources linked to Iran, reported possible US strikes on Qeshm in response to the Bahrain attack. The IRGC separately claimed it shot down an MQ-1 drone south of Qeshm. None of the Qeshm claims has been confirmed by Washington.
On diplomacy, the gap is widening rather than closing. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Oman's Badr Albusaidi in Muscat on Tuesday; Oman's Foreign Ministry said they discussed protecting "maritime corridors" and reviving dialogue, but its statement named neither the Strait of Hormuz nor the United States, and announced no agreement, no visit and no next meeting. A Qatari delegation also met Iranian negotiators on Tuesday in an undisclosed location, according to Traders Union. Pakistan's foreign minister said on Monday that Washington has still not replied to Iran's proposal on the strait, and Iran's parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, wrote on Tuesday that Iran will now treat any dam, port or power plant near a US or Israeli base as "dual-use" — civilian and military at once. Tehran has ruled out curbs on uranium enrichment and IAEA access to damaged nuclear sites, while Trump has said further strikes on Iran are "quite unlikely" and the military part of the war is "effectively over," and Vice President JD Vance has said it will not become a "forever war." Trump has said Iran will come up when he meets Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on Thursday.
In Yemen, the Houthis are now about 60 km from Aden, holding positions at the Al-Kharaz camp in Al-Mudharaba after government forces withdrew from Bab el-Mandeb, according to sources cited by AFP. Yemeni military sources told Reuters on Monday that Houthi fighters had reached Khor Omairh, about 100 km west of Aden, and were 25 km from government lines at Qawah. The toll from a Houthi missile attack on a checkpoint in Lahij on Sunday rose to eight dead and 12 wounded. Saudi Arabia replaced its coalition commander on Monday, moving Lieutenant General Fahd bin Hamad Al-Salman to an advisory role and giving Chief of the General Staff Fayyad Al-Ruwaili command of the joint forces — a change two Western diplomats linked directly to the battlefield setbacks. Senior Houthi official Hussein al-Ezzi said the movement does not intend to advance further toward Aden. The Houthis also claimed on Sunday to have hit King Khalid International Airport and a financial centre in Riyadh with two ballistic missiles; the coalition said it intercepted two Houthi drones over the Mecca and Riyadh regions on Monday.
For ordinary people, the disconnect between the battlefield and the market is still the story. Brent crude fell to about $91.66 a barrel early on Tuesday on the IEA's forecast of a 1.7-million-barrel-a-day global surplus this quarter, then bounced back toward $93.50 as reports of the Qeshm strikes hit, according to XTB — the market is swinging on each new incident. Traffic through the strait is still only about 49% of its pre-war level, and the human cost is concentrated in Yemen, where more than 348,000 people have been displaced since August 1.
In short: a fourth tanker burned in Hormuz in under 24 hours, Iran hit at Bahrain again and US strikes on Qeshm Island were reported but not confirmed, Muscat produced no deal, and the Houthis sit about 60 km from Aden after Saudi Arabia changed its coalition commander. Watch whether Washington confirms the Qeshm strikes, whether the tanker attacks continue, and Thursday's Shenzhen trilateral, where Trump says he will raise Iran.
Sources:
Source: silentdossier.com.

item.title: Nvidia's first report without Huang beats everything — and the board says he's not coming back
item.description:
Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion on Tuesday, up 103% from a year earlier and well above the $109.1 billion Wall Street expected, in its first earnings since co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on November 12 — and the board used the earnings call to close the door on his return. Adjusted earnings were $2.68 a share against a $2.47 consensus, and the company guided fourth-quarter revenue to $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, above the roughly $125 billion analysts expected. Shares, which closed the regular session at $155.46, down 0.4% on the day, rose roughly 3–4% in after-hours trading.
The details, as reported by MLQ.ai, CNBC via MLQ, Reuters and the Motley Fool: data centre revenue rose 110% to $107.6 billion — hyperscale sales of $60.1 billion, up 71%, and AI clouds, industrial and enterprise sales of $47.5 billion, up 195%. GAAP net income was $65.3 billion, GAAP diluted EPS $2.70, and gross margin was 74.8%. Chair Harvey Jones opened the 5 p.m. ET call by saying Huang resigned on November 12 "after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms," and that "the Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Hours earlier, Huang had said he would be honoured to return if asked. Jones said the board has retained Heidrick & Struggles for the CEO search and is considering internal and external candidates: "We want to install the CEO, the permanent CEO, as quickly as possible. But we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person." Interim CEO Colette Kress raised the fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to about 75%, up from the 70% forecast in August, and said it is "business as usual," with customers, suppliers and partners "100% behind us." She also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper products to China, and the fourth-quarter outlook assumes no data centre compute revenue from China.
The arguments split two ways. The bull case is the numbers themselves: revenue more than doubled, the beat was on every headline metric, Vera Rubin is shipping and Nvidia called it the fastest product ramp in its history, and Kress raised the long-term growth outlook. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co. said, "Strong guide and many did not expect that." The bear case, as the Motley Fool put it, is that the guidance is softer than it looks — the fourth quarter is a 14-week quarter, so spread across 14 weeks it implies weekly revenue up only about 4% from the third quarter — and gross margin is guided down to 71–72%. Growth is also tying up cash: accounts receivable reached $81.0 billion, or 64 days of sales, up from 60 days, and the Fool noted receivables rose about $18 billion in the quarter, nearly matching the revenue increase. And the leadership question, while answered for now, is not settled: the board's investigation into the reports that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation continues, and the board said it would take no questions on the circumstances of the resignation.
For ordinary people, the stakes are mostly in retirement accounts and the broader market: Nvidia is the world's third-largest company and the anchor of the AI rally, and the stock had fallen about 30% in a month to its lowest since July 1, 2025, before this report. The after-hours bounce is relief, not resolution — the stock is still down roughly 27% over the past month and about 36% below its October record of $243.37. The next tests are whether a permanent CEO is named, what the board's investigation finds, and whether receivables keep growing as fast as revenue.
In short: Nvidia beat on revenue, earnings and guidance in its first report without Huang, raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to ~75%, and the board said plainly it does not intend to reinstate him — and the market rewarded it with a 3–4% after-hours rise. Watch the CEO search, the investigation's findings, and Wednesday's regular-session open for whether the bounce holds.
Sources:
Source: g.foolcdn.com.

item.title: Apple outage: iCloud, App Store and Apple Music went down Tuesday — Apple blames an internal update, not a cyberattack:
item.description:
Apple users began reporting problems across several services on Tuesday, including iCloud, the App Store and Apple Music.
Apple's System Status page acknowledged disruptions, saying affected services "may be slow or unavailable," with iCloud Account & Sign In and AppleCare on Device listed as affecting all users. Users reported being unexpectedly signed out of iCloud and hitting verification errors trying to sign back in.
The AppleCare problem began around 11:15 a.m. ET, the others around 11:45 a.m.
ET. Apple later told Bloomberg the outages were due to an unspecified internal update and said they were largely resolved; there is no evidence of a cyberattack.
(NorthJersey · MacRumors)
Source: northjersey.com.

item.title: Google Wallet comes to iPhone in the US — but without tap to pay:
item.description:
Google said on Tuesday it is bringing Google Wallet to iOS in the United States, for payments and managing purchases across Google services.
Apple has allowed NFC contactless payments in third-party apps since iOS 18.1, but only under a commercial agreement with Apple, which is likely why Google has not implemented tap to pay. (MacRumors)
Source: macrumors.com.

item.title: Apple reportedly close to a long-term Samsung memory deal:
item.description:
Apple is close to signing a four-to-five-year DRAM supply agreement with Samsung, running from the first half of 2027, that would guarantee minimum volumes but leave pricing to market conditions, according to South Korea's Maeil Business Newspaper.
The report also says Apple recently reached a separate long-term deal with SK Hynix. Neither company has confirmed the agreement, so treat it as reported, not done.
It matters because memory prices are squeezing Apple's costs — memory's share of iPhone Pro material costs rose from about 10% to 34% in a year, per TrendForce — and Apple has warned Mac and iPad supply could stay constrained through the holiday quarter. (The Apple Post)
Source: theapplepost.com.

item.title: CISA added Puppet Enterprise RCE CVE-2026-115731 to KEV today:
item.description:
CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 17, with a federal remediation deadline of December 1.
It is a deserialization bug (CVSS 9.4) in Puppet Enterprise's report-processing code: any machine with a CA-signed agent certificate can send a crafted report and run code on the Puppet Server. Perforce fixed it on November 3 in Puppet Enterprise 2023.8.13, 2025.12.1 and 2026.0.1, along with a second critical bug, CVE-2026-115732, a certificate-name authorization bypass that was not added to KEV.
Open-source Puppet has no fix. CISA has not said who is exploiting it.
The KEV catalog now stands at 1,782 entries. (Corgea · Undercode News · Carthage Electronics)
Source: corgea.com.

item.title: Apache HTTP/2 flaw CVE-2026-119618 is now reportedly being exploited:
item.description:
Singapore's Cyber Security Agency told organisations on November 17 to patch, saying the flaw in mod_http2 is "reportedly being actively exploited, and a proof-of-concept exploit is publicly available."
That updates this morning's brief, which said there was no known in-the-wild exploitation. The flaw was fixed in Apache 2.4.71 on November 11 and affects versions 2.4.55–2.4.70 with HTTP/2 enabled.
It was still not listed in CISA's KEV catalog as of 12:25 UTC on Tuesday. (RecaTools)
Source: recatools.com.

item.title: Israel's opposition takes the speaker's chair — and Netanyahu's grip slips
item.description:
Israel's parliament voted on Tuesday to install Matan Kahana of Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party as Knesset speaker, replacing Amir Ohana of Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud, in the opposition bloc's first major move since the October 27 election stripped Netanyahu of his majority. Kahana won 66 votes to 52 for Likud's candidate, coalition whip Ofir Katz, after a stormy seven-hour debate — and the vote hands the bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu control of the legislative agenda before a new government is even formed.
The details, as reported by Reuters, CNN and AP: lawmakers voted separately on each candidate rather than in a head-to-head ballot. Kahana was backed by the Jewish-led opposition parties and by the Arab-led parties — the opposition holds 67 seats in the 120-member chamber, including 48 across four Jewish parties and a record 19 for the two Arab parties, the Joint List and Raam. In his first comments as speaker, Kahana struck a conciliatory note: "The Knesset of Israel is the home of all the citizens of the state of Israel, and I intend to be the speaker of everyone." He also said he would abide by the decisions of the Supreme Court. The Eisenkot bloc has already appointed interim chairs for key Knesset committees, including finance and defence, and Avigdor Liberman, now chairing the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, has said he will summon all the security chiefs for briefings. Special committees have been set up to repeal a bill that changed how judges are selected and legislation that limits the attorney general, and to undo a media regulation overhaul; the bloc has also pledged to establish a state commission of inquiry into the failures behind the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack, which Netanyahu has refused to investigate.
The two sides read the vote very differently. Eisenkot called Kahana's appointment "a proper democratic move which reflects the absolute majority who voted for change," and the bloc's priorities — term limits for the prime minister, a state inquiry into October 7, and rolling back the 2023 judicial overhaul that sparked nationwide protests — are now on the table. Likud condemned the outcome as "a low point in the history of the Knesset," saying Kahana was elected with "the votes of terror supporters," and during the debate members of Netanyahu's bloc shouted "shame" at each Arab lawmaker who voted for Kahana. Netanyahu has spent the campaign attacking Israel's Arab-led parties as an existential threat, and has baselessly alleged voter fraud by Arabs; election officials say they have seen no evidence of fraud that could have influenced the outcome. Analysts quoted by AP caution that time is short: the speaker can make the legislative process much faster or slower, but bills must be introduced, considered in committee and voted on several times before passing, and Eisenkot has only about four and a half to five more weeks to form a government. The obstacles are real — Liberman has vetoed any government that relies on Arab parties' support and is pushing talks with the ultra-Orthodox parties instead, former prime minister Naftali Bennett reportedly favours a unity government with Likud, and Netanyahu has conditioned any talks on remaining prime minister, which Eisenkot has rejected. If no one can form a government, another election will be held next year.
For ordinary people, the vote is about who controls the rules of Israeli democracy for the next few years: whether the judicial overhaul laws are repealed, whether there is finally an independent inquiry into October 7, and whether the Knesset's agenda is set by Netanyahu's caretaker government or by the bloc that beat him at the ballot box. The scars of October 7 were on display in the chamber itself — Likud member Talik Gvili, whose son was a police officer killed by Palestinian militants on October 7, interrupted Joint List member Ahmad Tibi mid-speech, shouting "Who killed my son?" and Tibi replied from the dais: "The one who committed the murder is Hamas. The one responsible is your prime minister."
In short: Kahana's 66–52 win gives the opposition control of the Knesset's agenda and committees, with judicial-overhaul repeal and an October 7 inquiry as its first targets — but Eisenkot still has to form a government within about five weeks, and his own bloc is split over how. Watch the committee moves this week and whether the ultra-Orthodox parties open talks with Eisenkot.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Trump in Manila:
item.description:
Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday for his first trip abroad since the midterm elections, joining the Quad meeting — the US, Japan, Australia and India — for the first time in two years, plus a US-ASEAN special summit and an ASEAN gala where he is guest of honour.
He is set to sign a trade deal with Thailand on Tuesday and meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Wednesday, before heading to Shenzhen for Thursday's trilateral with Xi and Putin. (AP · Reuters)
Source: krvs.org.

item.title: Kyiv's bridges partly reopened:
item.description:
Kyiv partially restored traffic over the Southern and Northern bridges on Tuesday after the overnight missile strikes.
Trams and trolleybuses are back on regular routes; the Southern Bridge is open to limited one-way traffic from the Left Bank to the Right Bank (vehicles up to 10 tonnes, public transport up to 18 tonnes, at controlled intervals), while the Northern Bridge and the eastern-bank Green Line metro services remain closed. Some districts have been switched to backup heating, with hot water temporarily unavailable in affected areas.
(h.ua · Kyiv Post)
Source: en.h.ua.

item.title: France confirmed its "Volia" training mission in Ukraine:
item.description:
France has acknowledged that military personnel have been present in Ukraine for several months under the mission name "Volia," training troops and maintaining French-supplied weapons and equipment.
French officials say the rotating groups do not take part in combat; Russian officials call the mission direct involvement in the war and have threatened French personnel. This confirms the single-source RFI report from November 16.
(h.ua)
Source: en.h.ua.

item.title: Bridges on both sides: Ukraine collapses the Kerch road span as Russia hits Kyiv's crossings
item.description:
Ukraine severely damaged the bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea overnight, collapsing a section of its road span, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky called an "unprecedented" operation — while Russia answered by firing seven ballistic missiles at two of Kyiv's main bridges across the Dnipro, killing at least two people in the capital and knocking out power, water and heating. It was the second straight night of record-scale drone warfare on both sides, and it landed on the morning of the Ramstein defence meeting in Brussels and two days before Thursday's Trump–Putin–Xi summit in Shenzhen.
The details, as reported by the Press Association, Reuters and Ukrainian officials: Ukraine's General Staff said an arch and a span of the Kerch Bridge's road section collapsed, severing the road link, while the railway line was still standing but its arch was damaged. Zelensky said the attack was the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes in seven stages — knocking out air defences, radars and electronic-warfare equipment first — before domestically built long-range drones hit the road section and Neptune missiles and other drones targeted the rail section, with Flamingo precision-guided missiles delivering the final blow. Russia's Investigative Committee said the bridge was attacked by drones and sustained damage; Crimea's Moscow-installed governor, Sergei Aksyonov, said traffic was halted but rail traffic was restored by Tuesday afternoon, without mentioning damage. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said there was "no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than it was before." Russia's Defence Ministry said its air defences downed 1,441 Ukrainian drones overnight — a day after claiming 1,336, the previous record — and Moscow's mayor said around 800 drones flew toward the capital region, 321 shot down as they approached. Independent outlet Astra reported a huge fire at the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat petrochemical complex in Bashkortostan, nearly 1,300 km from the border.
In Kyiv, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles hit the Southern Bridge and three hit the Northern Bridge. Both were closed to traffic, the metro system was partially damaged, and fires broke out in four districts. Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported two deaths in Kyiv's Obolonskyi district. Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said overnight strikes left consumers without power in eight Ukrainian regions; Zelensky put the figure at significant outages in three regions. Russian strikes also hit Zaporizhzhia, killing two people and wounding 18, and industrial facilities in three districts of the region. The Russian Defence Ministry confirmed strikes on Ukrainian transport, energy, military and port infrastructure.
The two sides are telling very different stories about what this means. Kyiv frames the Kerch strike as a masterstroke against the symbol of Russia's 2014 annexation — the General Staff's statement was blunt: "The symbol of the occupation has cracked." UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, meeting allies at NATO headquarters in Brussels, called it "another example of Ukrainian ingenuity and Ukraine's absolute determination to defend itself." Moscow, for its part, treats the bridge as repairable and the Kyiv strikes as routine — its Defence Ministry described the overnight barrage as a strike on military-industrial, energy, transport and port infrastructure, and Peskov promised a better bridge. Zelensky, meanwhile, said Russia has battered Ukrainian infrastructure, especially the power grid, every day, and that "we have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation — and every proposal has been met with loud rejection." He also said on Monday that Russia is receiving dozens of ballistic missiles from North Korea every month and urged allies to give Ukraine comparable weapons for "missile parity." On diplomacy, the negotiating teams of Ukraine, the US and European partners held a working video call on Monday about the Abu Dhabi talks and next steps; Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, said "we aligned our positions and our next joint steps." The US was represented by envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and the commander of US forces in Europe, Alexus Grynkewich.
For ordinary people, this is now a war on the routes they use every day. In Kyiv, two of the eight bridges across the Dnipro are shut, buses and trolleybuses have been diverted, the metro is partly damaged, and parts of the city are without water, power and heating as winter closes in. In Crimea, the road link that moves military and civilian supplies to the peninsula is severed, at least for now. And in Russia, the drone war is reaching deeper — Bashkortostan is nearly 1,300 km from Ukraine's border. The immediate test is today in Brussels: Germany's Defence Minister Boris Pistorius announced a $300 million contribution to NATO's PURL programme for US weapons for Ukraine — its fifth package — focused on PAC-2 and PAC-3 Patriot missiles, with Germany and Norway sponsoring the package. Patriot missiles are the only weapon reliable enough to stop Russian ballistic missiles, but there is a global shortage, made worse since the US launched its war against Iran. Germany is also working to integrate its IRIS-T missile with Norwegian NASAMS systems and will deliver additional radars, drone ammunition and fighter jets. NATO allies will also discuss Washington's review of US troop levels in Europe with Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, who is attending the Ramstein meeting; more clarity on any drawdown is expected within weeks.
In short: both sides struck the other's bridges overnight — Ukraine collapsed part of the Kerch road span after weeks of preparation, Russia hit Kyiv's North and South bridges with seven ballistic missiles and cut power in eight regions — in the biggest drone exchange of the war so far. Watch today's Ramstein meeting for Patriot missiles, and Thursday's Shenzhen trilateral, where Trump says he will raise Ukraine with Xi and Putin even though US officials say it is not on the agenda.
Sources:
Source: content.assets.pressassociation.io.

item.title: Two more tankers hit in Hormuz as the US and Iran trade blows — and oil falls anyway
item.description:
The Gulf war's sharpest escalation in days came on Sunday night and Monday, with two more tankers confirmed hit in the Strait of Hormuz, a US strike on Iranian missile launchers reported but not confirmed by Washington, a drone alarm at Iraq's biggest gas field, and the Houthis closing in on Aden — yet oil prices fell, not rose, as traders bet on a global supply surplus.
The details, as reported by Reuters and Al Jazeera: the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency confirmed two tanker attacks in the strait on Monday. In the latest, a tanker was disabled and an engine-room fire broke out after an attack seven nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman; earlier, another tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile while travelling out of the strait, also causing an engine-room fire. No casualties were reported in either. Maritime monitor Vanguard identified the first vessel as the Panama-flagged On Phoenix, hit about three nautical miles off Oman. Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Navy said two oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire while trying to cross the southern part of the strait through a route Tehran considers unauthorised, and Iran's regular navy said another tanker caught fire and was immobilised after hitting a mine east of the strait — bringing the Guard's claimed tally to six tankers on fire since Sunday. None of the Iranian mine claims has been independently verified, and Iranian authorities have not identified the vessels. The Guard also said it seized a US MQ-170 drone near Qeshm Island after an electronic-warfare operation; that claim is also unverified. Euronews reported that the US military launched airstrikes on Iranian missile launchers at Bandar Lengeh and Sirik in southern Iran on Sunday night, after Iranian forces attacked a US base in Bahrain and fired on tankers — but US Central Command has not confirmed the strikes, and other outlets note the report cites no confirming source. Iran did carry out a drone attack on a radar at the US Al Riffa air base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second in three days; Bahrain and Washington say every drone was shot down, with no injuries or damage. The USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the region over the weekend, joining the USS George Washington and USS George H.W. Bush — three US carrier strike groups in the Middle East for the first time since the Iraq war.
The fighting is also spreading inland. In Iraq's Kurdistan region, warning sirens sounded on Monday after a drone flew over the Khor Mor gas field, Reuters reported, citing two security sources. There were no immediate reports of a strike or damage — but production at Khor Mor had already been halted the previous week after a suspected drone attack sparked a fire and knocked out 2.8 gigawatts of electricity generation, according to Dana Gas, one of the field's operators. The field supplies most of the natural gas for power generation in Iraqi Kurdistan, and Kurdish officials have blamed Iranian-backed armed groups for repeated attacks on it. No group was identified as responsible for Monday's flyover. In Yemen, the Houthis have advanced to about 60 km from Aden after government-aligned forces withdrew from positions overlooking the Bab al-Mandeb Strait to reinforce the city's defence; the Houthis now control the area overlooking the strategic waterway. The International Organization for Migration said at least 348,000 people have been displaced in fighting between Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis since August 1, including 18,780 between November 8 and 14. Saudi Arabia replaced the commander of its coalition forces in Yemen on Monday, appointing General Fayyad al-Ruwaili in place of Lieutenant General Fahd bin Hamad al-Salman. The Houthis claimed Saudi forces launched 88 airstrikes and missile attacks in 24 hours against Sanaa and several governorates; those claims have not been independently verified.
The two sides' positions are hardening in opposite directions. Tehran is floating a two-day plan to reopen Hormuz — Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, in Muscat on Tuesday after an Economic Cooperation Organisation meeting in Islamabad, said the organisation welcomed the proposal — but it is conditional on Washington accepting Iran's terms, and Tehran has ruled out curbs on uranium enrichment and IAEA access to damaged nuclear sites. Iran also warned vessels against entering areas it considers unauthorised and said ships must coordinate with its armed forces. Washington, for its part, has not confirmed the reported Sunday-night strikes, and Vice President JD Vance said there was no disagreement between him and President Trump over Iran, acknowledging the political cost of higher energy prices but saying the conflict would not become a "forever war." Trump has said further strikes on Iran are "quite unlikely" and that the military part of the war is "effectively over" — even as the fighting widens.
For ordinary people, the disconnect between the battlefield and the market is the story. Brent crude fell to about $91.66–$91.80 a barrel on Tuesday, down roughly 0.8%, with WTI around $85, despite the fresh tanker attacks — the IEA said on Friday that the global oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter, with supply running about 1.7 million barrels a day above demand, and Middle East exports recovering faster than demand. Traffic through the strait is still only about 49% of its pre-war level, according to ANZ bank estimates, and marine underwriters have repriced transit exposure to near-prohibitive levels. The human cost is concentrated in Yemen, where more than a third of a million people have been displaced since August, and in Iraqi Kurdistan, where the Khor Mor shutdown has already cut power generation. Iran is also facing warnings of winter gas shortages, with its government forecasting a peak-demand deficit of about 430 million cubic metres per day.
In short: two tankers were confirmed hit in Hormuz on Monday, Iran claims six on fire since Sunday (unverified), the US is reported to have struck missile launchers at Bandar Lengeh and Sirik (unconfirmed by CENTCOM), a drone buzzed Iraq's Khor Mor gas field, and the Houthis are closing on Aden — but oil fell anyway on surplus forecasts. Watch Araghchi's talks in Muscat today, and whether CENTCOM confirms the Sunday-night strikes.
Sources:
Source: aljazeera.com.
